en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory!
Janamejaya said:
When Duryodhana had been slain and the entire army destroyed,
O sage, what did the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra do upon hearing this? And likewise, what did the Kuru king, the high-minded son of Dharma, do?
And what did those three—Kṛpa and the others—do?
We have heard of Aśvatthāman’s deed and the mutual curses they inflicted upon one another;
now tell us the subsequent account of what Sañjaya reported.
Vaiśampāyana said: When his hundred sons had been slain, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was dejected like a tree with its branches lopped off,
tormented by grief for his sons.
Having become mute through meditation and overwhelmed by anxiety, the highly wise Sañjaya approached him and spoke these words:
"Why do you grieve, O Great King? In grief there is no companion."
O lord of the people, eighteen akṣauhiṇīs have been slain;
this earth is now utterly empty, devoid of inhabitants, and solitary.
Having assembled from various directions, these lords of men from diverse lands [have perished].
Together with your son, they have all indeed met their end.
Perform the funeral rites for your fathers, sons, grandsons, kinsmen, friends,
and teachers in their proper order.
"And as for the other followers who have been slain,
O lord of men, perform all the funeral rites for them.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard those piteous words, Dhṛtarāṣṭra— afflicted by the slaughter of his sons and grandsons, though himself difficult to overcome— fell to the ground like a tree struck down by the wind. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
With my sons slain, my ministers slain, and all my friends and kinsmen slain,
I shall surely experience suffering as I wander this earth. What indeed is the use of life for me today, deprived as I am of my kin?

O one of great wisdom, like a bird whose wings have been clipped and who is worn out by old age, I shall no longer shine— having been stripped of my kingdom, deprived of my friends, and likewise robbed of my sight, like the sun when its rays have faded.
The words of my friends were not heeded— the chatter of the son of Jamadagni,
as well as that of the celestial sage Nārada and Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
nor was that which was spoken for my welfare by Kṛṣṇa in the midst of the assembly.
"O King, enough of this enmity; let your son be reconciled.
Because I, a man of evil intent, did not act upon those words, I now suffer greatly, for I did not listen to the righteous discourse spoken by Bhīṣma.
Having heard of the slaughter of Duḥśāsana and the downfall of Karṇa, as well as the death of Droṇa— who was like a bellowing bull—
and the solar eclipse, my heart is rent asunder.
"O Sañjaya, I do not recall any evil deed committed by me in the past,
the fruit of which is now being experienced here by this deluded man. Surely, some wrong must have been done by me in previous births."
By which the Ordainer has joined me to deeds that result in a share of suffering;
and the decline of my age, the destruction of all my kinsmen, and the loss of my well-wishers and friends have come upon me through the power of destiny.
"Who else in this world is more afflicted with suffering than I?
Therefore, let the Pāṇḍavas behold me this very day, firm in my vows,
having set out upon the long path toward the realm of Brahmā."
11,001.021 Vaiśampāyana said: While the king was thus lamenting and brooding over his great sorrow, Sañjaya spoke these words to dispel his grief.
"O King, dispel your grief; you have heard the definitive conclusions of the Vedas and various scriptural traditions from the elders, O best of monarchs—
those things which the sages spoke in the past to Sṛñjaya when he was afflicted by sorrow for his son."
O King, when your son had thus become possessed by the pride born of youth,
you did not heed the words of your well-wishers as they spoke;
being greedy and eager for the fruit [of your own gain], you accomplished no purpose for yourself.
By means of his own intellect alone, he acted with a single-edged sword;
for the most part, those devoid of virtuous conduct— your counselor Duḥśāsana and the evil-minded son of Rādhā— were constantly attended by him.
The evil-minded Śakuni, the wicked Citrasena,
and Śalya, by whom indeed the entire world was made like a thorn;
[and the words] of Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus, of Gāndhārī, and of Vidura—
O great king, [it was told] by Droṇa and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat;
by the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa and the wise Nārada;
and likewise by other ṛṣis and by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor.

O Bhārata, those words were not heeded by your son, who was small-minded, arrogant, and constantly proclaiming "war. Cruel, intolerant, ever-dissatisfied, yet full of prowess, he did not follow your advice.
"You are learned, wise, and always truthful.
Such virtuous and intelligent people as you do not lose their composure. It is not that you have ever honored righteousness by constantly saying, 'War is the way.'"
All the Kṣatriyas have been destroyed, and the fame of our enemies has increased. For you remained neutral and did not say anything appropriate;
as a bearer of the burden, you did not carry the weight with an even hand.
A person should act appropriately from the very beginning,
so that he is not later joined with remorse for a matter already past.
O King, out of greed for your son and desiring to do what was pleasing to him, you acted thus.
This remorse has now come upon you; you ought not to grieve. He who sees only the honey and does not perceive the precipice falls through his greed for the honey and grieves just as you do.
One who does not grieve attains his goals; one who does not grieve finds happiness. One who does not grieve attains prosperity; one who does not grieve finds the supreme.
It is like one who, having himself produced a fire, should then try to wrap it up in a cloth.
He who, being consumed by fire, experiences mental anguish is not a wise man.
By you alone, together with your son, this fire of Pārtha has been fanned by the wind of your words, sprinkled with the clarified butter of greed, and set ablaze.
When that fire was kindled, your sons fell into it like moths;
you ought not to grieve for them, consumed by the flames of Keśava. And as for the face you bear, O King, soiled with the falling of tears—
For the wise do not praise this which is seen to be contrary to the scriptures;
indeed, like sparks, these [passions] burn men. Therefore, abandon your anger through wisdom, and sustain yourself by means of your own self.
Thus consoled by that high-souled Sañjaya,
Vidura spoke once more with deliberate intent, O scorcher of foes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, gladdening that bull among men with words like nectar, Vidura spoke to the son of Vicitravīrya; learn what he said. Vidura said:
"Arise, O King! Why do you lie there? Support yourself by your own self!
This is the inevitable end for all mortals, both the stationary and the moving.
O Lord of the World, this indeed is the ultimate destiny of all living beings."

All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation, for life indeed ends in death. O Bhārata, when Yama drags away both the hero and the coward alike, [what need is there for weapons?]
"O bull among kṣatriyas, why then will those kṣatriyas not fight?
One dies without fighting, and one lives by fighting;
O great king, when the time has arrived, no one can transcend it."
O Bhārata, the elements begin in non-existence, have existence as their middle state, and end indeed in non-existence;
what cause for lamentation is there in this? By grieving, a man does not follow the dead, nor by grieving does he himself die.
In this world which is thus established by nature, why do you grieve?
Time drags away all beings of every kind;
no one is dear to Time, nor is anyone hateful, O best of the Kurus.
Just as the wind sweeps away the tips of blades of grass in every direction,
so too, O bull among the Bharatas, do all beings fall under the power of Time.
For all those traveling together in a single caravan toward that same destination, [the end is the same].
When time passes before one, what cause for lamentation is there?
O King, you ought not to grieve for those slain in battle,
if the scriptures are your authority, for they have attained the supreme goal.
For all were devoted to sacred study, and all had observed their vows;
all have passed away facing toward [the goal]. What cause for lamentation is there in that?
Having come from the unseen, they have once again gone to the unseen.
They are not yours, nor are you theirs; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Even if slain, one attains heaven; by slaying, one gains glory.
Both outcomes are highly beneficial for us; there is no fruitlessness in battle.
Indra will intend for them worlds that yield all desires;
for they, O bull among men, become the guests of Indra—
not by sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, nor by austerities, nor by learning.
In this way, mortals go to heaven, just as heroes slain in battle do;
they offered oblations of arrows into the fires of the bodies of the brave,
and those radiant warriors consumed the arrows being offered to one another.
"O King, thus I have described to you the supreme path leading to heaven.
For a Kṣatriya in this world, there is nothing superior to battle.
Those Kṣatriyas were high-souled, heroic, and ornaments of the assembly."
The highest blessings have been attained; indeed, none of them are to be mourned. Having comforted yourself by means of your own self, do not grieve, O bull among men;
you ought not to abandon your duty today while overcome by sorrow.

Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, have been experienced throughout the cycles of existence; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong? There are thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for fear.
Day after day, these afflictions enter the fool, but not the wise man.
O best of the Kurus, there is no one dear to Time, nor anyone hated;
Time is never indifferent toward anyone—it drags everything away.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome.
Life, physical form, youth, and the accumulation of wealth are all impermanent.

A wise person should not crave health or the company of loved ones; you ought not to grieve alone for the suffering of the people, for even through their disappearance, that suffering does not cease for you.
One should not grieve, but should act if one perceives the possibility of remedial effort;
this is the medicine for suffering: that one should not dwell upon it. For when it is dwelt upon, it does not depart, but rather increases all the more.
Due to union with the undesired and separation from the beloved,
those of small intellect suffer through the failure to obtain what they have not yet gained and the loss of what they have already obtained; such humans are joined with mental sufferings.

There is neither wealth, nor merit, nor happiness for one who grieves over this; yet he does not cease from his pursuit of worldly affairs, and thus he falls away from the three goals of life. Indeed, men encounter various and distinct states of wealth.
Those who are discontented become deluded; the wise attain contentment.
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom and physical suffering with medicines.
This is the power of knowledge; one should not equate it with that of the ignorant.
Karma follows a person who has acted in the past: it lies down with him when he lies down, stands by him when he stands, and runs after him when he runs.
In whatever state one performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [that karma follows].
In each respective state, one experiences that particular fruit;
with whichever body a person performs whatever action,
with that very same body they experience that particular fruit.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self;
for the self alone is the witness of one's own deeds, both those done and those left undone.
Happiness arises from virtuous action, and suffering from sinful action.
What has been done must be experienced everywhere; nowhere is what has not been done ever consumed.
For wise men like you do not become attached to actions that are contrary to knowledge, fraught with many calamities, and destructive to their very roots.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O man of great wisdom, this grief of mine has been dispelled by your well-spoken words. Nevertheless, I wish to hear further words from you according to the truth."
"By avoiding contact with the undesirable and by abandoning the desirable,
how indeed are the wise here liberated from mental sufferings?
Vidura said:
From whatever [object] the mind is liberated, whether from suffering or even from pleasure,
by attaining tranquility through that very means, the wise man finds a happy rebirth.
O bull among men, all this is impermanent when it is reflected upon.
The world is like a plantain tree; indeed, it possesses no core.
When both the wise and the foolish, the wealthy and the poor, all come under the power of the ancestors, they sleep, free from their feverish anxieties.
With limbs devoid of flesh, consisting mostly of bone, and bound together by sinews—
what distinction do other people perceive therein by which they might recognize a difference in lineage or physical form?
Why do men of deluded intellect desire one another? For the wise say that the houses of mortals are indeed their bodies; they are all separated by time, but the single essence alone is beautiful.
Just as a man, having cast off a garment that is either worn out or unworn,
chooses another garment, so too are the bodies of embodied beings.
O son of Vicitravīrya, whether it be a dwelling or whether it be suffering or happiness, [it is the same].
In this world, living beings experience the results of their own actions alone.
By means of action, O Bhārata, one attains heaven, happiness, and suffering;
therefore, whether against one's will or by one's own choice, one must bear that burden.
Just as a vessel made of clay, mounted upon a wheel, may perish—
whether while it is being fashioned, or immediately after it has been finished,
or when it is broken, or while it is being lowered, or even once it has descended.
Whether wet or dry, while being cooked, or even as it is being removed from the oven,
or once taken out, O Bhārata,
or even while being consumed— such is the state of the bodies of embodied beings.
Whether still in the womb, or already born, or a day old; or having passed half a month, or even a full month;
or a year old, or even two years old—
Whether one is in the prime of youth, in middle age, or even old, one meets with misfortune.
Beings come into existence and cease to exist due to their past actions.
Since this world is established by such natural necessity, for what reason do you grieve?
And just as, O King, some creature moving about in the water for the sake of sport might emerge and submerge, O lord of men,
so too [is it] from the emergence and submersion within the thicket of saṃsāra.
Those of small intelligence, bound by the experience of karma, suffer;
but the great seers have crossed over by means of the vast yoga of knowledge. Those who are wise, established in truth, are seekers of the end of saṃsāra.
"Those who understand the meeting of all beings attain the supreme goal.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O best of speakers, how is the thicket of saṃsāra to be understood?"
"I wish to hear this; tell the truth to me who asks.
Vidura said:
"O Lord, listen to all the activities of living beings from their very birth."
Previously, he dwells here for a short while within the *kalala*;
then, by the force of the wind, he remains for a short while more in the *kalala*.
Then, when the fifth month has passed, he brings forth flesh.
Then, at the end of the month, the fetus, with all its limbs fully formed, comes forth.
It dwells in the midst of impurity, smeared with flesh and blood;
then, by the force of the wind, it is turned so that its feet are upward and its head is downward.
Having reached the door of the womb, he encounters many afflictions; indeed, due to the compression of the womb, he is tormented by his past karmas.
Released from that, he perceives other calamities within the cycle of existence.
The planets approach him like dogs approaching meat;
then, when the time has arrived, diseases likewise approach him while he is still living, being bound by his own past actions.
O lord of men, for one who is bound by the snares of the senses— snares that are sweet with attachment— and is thus afflicted, various calamities draw near;
and being bound by them again and again, he never attains satisfaction.
Then, while performing both good and evil deeds, he does not perceive them;
likewise, those who are fully established in meditation protect him,
so that for the time being he does not realize that the realm of Yama has arrived.

Dragged away by the messengers of Yama, he goes toward death in the course of time. Whatever pleasant or unpleasant words were uttered from the mouth of one devoid of speech, he later looks on with indifference as his very self binds himself.
Alas! The world is deceived and brought under the sway of greed;
intoxicated by greed, anger, and pride, it does not recognize its own true nature. Delighting in its own noble birth, it reviles those of low birth.
Proud with the arrogance of wealth, he reviles the poor;
he calls others fools but does not examine himself. He casts blame upon the instruction of others but does not wish to discipline himself.
When both the wise and the foolish, the wealthy and the destitute,
the high-born and the low-born, the proud and the humble alike—
having all reached the cemetery, they sleep there, stripped of their skin.
With limbs devoid of flesh, consisting mostly of bone, and bound together by sinews—
what distinction do other people perceive therein by which they might recognize a difference in lineage or physical form?
When all have been laid down equally and sleep upon the surface of the earth,
why do the foolish here desire to deceive one another? Having heard this scripture, both directly and indirectly...
In this unstable world of living beings, he who, observing the dharma,
conducts himself from birth onwards shall attain the supreme goal. Indeed,
having understood all this, he who follows that truth [attains it].
O lord of men, he obtains the path to liberation.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"This which is the dense thicket of dharma is being pursued with the intellect."
"Explain to me in full detail this entire path of wisdom.
Vidura said:
"In this regard, having paid homage to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), I shall describe it to you."
11,005.002c Just as the supreme sages describe the thicket of saṃsāra,
11,005.003a it is said that once a certain twice-born man, while wandering in this vast saṃsāra,
11,005.003c reached a great, impenetrable forest teeming with carnivorous beasts.

It was completely surrounded on all sides by those of terrifying appearance and fierce forms— having the shapes of lions, tigers, and elephants, exceedingly hideous, great devourers, flesh-eaters, and most fearsome— who inspired dread even in Death himself.
Seeing that heart of his, O scorcher of foes, he was seized by supreme agitation; indeed, there was a bristling of his hair and great physical transformations,
O Bhārata, as trembling came over his limbs and his hair stood on end.

11,005.006a Pursuing that forest, running hither and thither, 11,005.006c he looked in all directions, wondering where there might be refuge. 11,005.007a Seeking their vulnerability, he fled, tormented by fear.
He did not indeed go far away, nor was he separated from them;
then he beheld a terrible forest surrounded on all sides by snares,
embraced on both arms by an exceedingly horrific woman.
That great forest was surrounded by five-headed serpents like towering mountains, and by massive trees that touched the sky;
and in the midst of that forest there was a well covered over.
Covered and concealed by creepers hidden beneath a layer of grass,
that bird fell there into the secret pool of water;
he became entangled within that thicket of spreading vines.
Just as a large panasa fruit is born attached by its stalk,
so he hangs there with his feet upward and his head downward;
then, even there, another affliction arose for him once more.
In that very place, the elephant Dantī, who had shattered mountains, arrived; there he beheld a mighty great nāga in the middle of the well. At the edge of the well's rim, he saw the great elephant.
[He saw] one with six faces, black and variegated, moving upon twelve feet;
crawling in succession over places covered with creepers and trees.
And [he saw him] hanging from the branches of trees upon its own branches.
11,005.015c Bees of various forms, terrible in appearance and inspiring fear,
11,005.015e sit there having already gathered honey, dwelling in their own homes.
11,005.016a Again and again they strive for more honey, O bull of the Bharatas.
From those honey-streams, which are delicious to all beings and by which even a child is never satiated,
a flow pours forth constantly in many ways;
hanging down, that man drinks that stream forever.
And even as he drank in that perilous place, his thirst was not quenched;
unsatisfied, he constantly craved it again and again,
O King, and no weariness with life ever arose within him.
And upon that very tree was established a man’s hope for life; black and white mice were gnawing at that tree,
while wild beasts roamed the edge of the forest thicket and a most fierce woman dwelt there.
There is danger from a serpent beneath the well, and from an elephant at its mouth;
there is danger from falling from a tree, and fifthly, from mice.
They say the sixth great danger arises from bees out of greed for honey.
Thus he dwells there, cast into the ocean of saṃsāra; yet, because of his hope for life, he does not arrive at world-weariness. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Alas! He truly dwells in great suffering, living a life of hardship.
O best of speakers, how can he find pleasure or contentment there?
Where indeed is that place where he dwells in such a crisis of dharma?"
"How might that man be liberated from that great terror?
Tell me all of this; we shall act accordingly. For a great compassion has arisen in me for his deliverance."
Vidura said:
O King, this analogy has been cited by those who know liberation—
that by which a human being attains a happy state in the worlds beyond.

That which is called the great wilderness is indeed this saṃsāra; for that forest which is difficult to traverse is the dense thicket of saṃsāra. And those beasts of prey mentioned are proclaimed to be the diseases.
That large-bodied woman who presides there is indeed called Old Age by the wise, the destroyer of complexion and form;
and that well there, O King, is the body of embodied beings.
The great serpent who dwells there below is Time itself;
he is the Ender of all beings, the one who seizes away everything from those possessed of bodies.
And the creeper that grows in the middle of the pit is that very man.
That hope for life which hangs from the spreading branches belongs to embodied beings;
but he who creeps around that tree at the mouth of the well,
O King, is the six-faced elephant known as the year.
The seasons are said to be its faces, and the twelve months its feet. Those who contemplate the nature of beings declare that the days and nights are like mice that constantly gnaw at the tree.

Those bees there are proclaimed to be the objects of desire; and those many streams that flow with a honey-like distillation— one should know them to be the essences of desire, wherein human beings sink.
Those wise ones who thus understand the revolution of the wheel of saṃsāra truly sever the fetters of the wheel of saṃsāra;
for whomsoever disenchantment arises toward a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand [rebirths].
"Desires greatly delude the dull-witted who seek sense-objects.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Oh, what a well-spoken narrative you have related, O seer of reality!"
"Indeed, my joy increases all the more to hear the nectar of your speech.
Vidura said:
"Listen further; I shall explain in detail this path."
11,007.002c Having heard which, the wise are liberated from the cycles of existence.
11,007.003a Just as a man, O King, who has set out upon a long journey, 11,007.003c Stands still here and there out of fatigue, or even makes his dwelling;

Thus, O Bhārata, in the course of saṃsāra, within the various states of dwelling in the womb, the ignorant take up residence, while the wise are liberated therefrom. Therefore, those who know the scriptures call this very path "the road."
That which the wise call the dense forest of saṃsāra,
O bull of the Bharatas, is this very cycle of worlds for mortals—
both the moving and the stationary; a wise man should not crave it.

"O Bhārata, whatever diseases of mortals there may be— whether physical or mental, perceptible or imperceptible— they are described by the wise as 'venomous serpents' (vyāla). And being constantly tormented and struck down by them,"
Those of small intelligence are not terrified by their own karmas, which are like great,
venomous serpents. Yet even if a man should be liberated from those diseases, O King,
old age— which destroys beauty— will surely envelop him afterwards.
Sinking on all sides into a great mire without support— by means of sounds, forms, tastes, touches, and various scents as well—
the years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, nights, and their junctures [pass].
11,007.011c Gradually they plunder his form as well as his life-span. 11,007.012a These are the repositories of Time; the foolish do not understand them.
11,007.012c It is said that here all beings are inscribed by their own karma.
The body of living beings is said to be the chariot, while the quality of goodness (*sattva*) is called the charioteer. The senses are said to be the horses, and action and intellect are the reins.
He who follows the speed of those galloping horses is the self.
In this wheel of saṃsāra, one revolves like a wheel;
those who do not become deluded while wandering do not continue to wander in saṃsāra.
O King, for those who wander in saṃsāra, this very suffering arises.
Therefore, for the sake of its cessation, a wise person should indeed exert effort;
indifference should not be practiced here, for it grows with a hundred branches. O King, a man who has restrained his senses and cast out anger and greed [attains this].
He who is contented and speaks the truth attains peace.
He who restrains those senses by means of his intellect is a true driver; he does not turn back.
For they call this chariot "belonging to Yama," and by it the ignorant are deluded.
O King, O lord of men, he too shall experience that which you have now experienced,
O Bhārata— the loss of kingdom, the loss of friends, and the loss of sons. Indeed,
O Bhārata, this sorrow becomes all the more bitter when one has not yet quenched his thirst for worldly desires.
A virtuous person should apply the medicine for suffering against supreme miseries;
having obtained here the great medicine of knowledge, which reaches the far shore,
a man of restrained mind should cut away the great disease of suffering.
Neither prowess, nor wealth, nor a friend,
nor kinsmen can deliver one from suffering as effectively as a self established in firm restraint;
likewise, one's own mother, sons, and others cannot dispel sufferings.
Therefore, O Bhārata, having established yourself in loving-kindness and having undertaken moral conduct (*śīla*), self-restraint, renunciation, and vigilance— these three are the horses of Brahman.
He who stands upon the chariot of the mind, which is yoked with the reins of moral conduct, [reaches his goal].

O King, having abandoned the fear of death, he goes to the world of Brahmā. O Lord of the Earth, he who grants freedom from fear to all beings goes to the supreme station, the stainless abode of Viṣṇu.
Neither by a thousand sacrifices nor by constant fasts does a man obtain that fruit which he would attain through the gift of fearlessness;
for it is certain that among all beings there is nothing dearer than one's own self.
Death, O Bhārata, is undesirable to all living beings;
therefore, a wise person should practice compassion toward all creatures. They are shrouded by a web of intellect joined with various delusions.
Those of dull intellect and unrefined vision wander here and there; but the wise, possessing subtle vision, proceed to the eternal Brahman.
Knowing this, O man of great wisdom, perform for them the funeral rites.
"You ought to do this; by that very act, you shall indeed obtain the fruit of happiness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of Vidura, the best of the Kurus...
Tormented by grief for his son, he fell to the ground in a swoon. Seeing him thus fallen on the earth, unconscious, his kinsmen,
as well as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana and Vidura the steward, [approached].

O Bhārata, Sañjaya, his other friends, and those gatekeepers who were held in high esteem by him, touched his body with pleasantly cool water and fanned him diligently with palm-leaf fans. They also stroked his limbs with their hands as they attended to him with great care.
Having sat beside the Tathāgata Dhṛtarāṣṭra for a very long time,
the lord of the earth then regained consciousness after a long period and lamented for a long while, overwhelmed by the mental anguish caused by his sons.
"Fie upon human existence, and fie upon attachment to human things,
from which roots of sufferings arise again and again—
such as the loss of sons, the loss of wealth, and even the loss of kinsmen and relatives."
O Lord, one encounters a most great suffering comparable to poison or fire,
by which the limbs are consumed and by which wisdom is destroyed;
overcome by which, a person regards death as a blessing.
"O best of the twice-born, this calamity has befallen me through a reversal of fortune; I see no end to it except through the loss of my life, and that very thing I shall do this very day."
Having spoken thus to his high-souled father, the greatest knower of Brahman,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra became bewildered and fell into supreme grief;
O lord of the earth, that king remained silent, lost in thought.
Having heard those words of his, the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke these words to his son, who was tormented by grief for his sons:
"O mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listen to that which I shall say to you."
"You are learned and wise, as well as skilled in matters of dharma and worldly purpose.
O scorcher of foes, there is nothing further to be known that remains unknown to you. Indeed, you understand without doubt the impermanence of mortals."
Since the world of the living is unstable and one’s station is impermanent,
and since life ends in death, why do you grieve, O Bhārata?
O Indra among kings, the origin of this enmity was witnessed by you with your own eyes.
O King, making your son the cause, he was impelled by the power of time; and since this slaughter of the Kurus was inevitable,
why do you grieve for those heroes who have attained the supreme goal?
O mighty-armed lord of men, the high-souled Vidura, knowing [the truth],
strove with every effort for peace;
yet no one can alter a path ordained by destiny.
It is my conviction that even after striving for a long time, it is impossible to restrain them.
For I shall relate to you exactly what I have heard directly concerning the purpose of the gods, so that you may attain steadfastness.
Formerly, having overcome fatigue, I went in haste to the assembly hall of Indra; there I then beheld the inhabitants of heaven gathered together,
as well as all the celestial sages headed by Nārada.
And there, O Lord of the Earth, I also saw the Earth herself, who had arrived in the presence of the gods for a specific purpose. Then,
having approached the assembled deities, the nurse spoke to them.
"O highly fortunate ones, that task which was promised by you to me in the abode of Brahmā must now be swiftly accomplished.
Having heard those words of hers, Viṣṇu, who is honored by the worlds, [acted accordingly].
Laughing, he spoke these words to the Earth in the assembly of the gods:
"He who is indeed the eldest among the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
known as Duryodhana— he shall accomplish your task."
And having obtained that protector of the earth, you will have accomplished your purpose. For his sake, the rulers of the earth have assembled at Kurukṣetra;
striking with firm weapons, they shall slay one another.
"Then, O Goddess, there shall be for you the destruction of the burden in battle. Go quickly to your own place and sustain the worlds, O beautiful one.
This very son of yours, O King, was born for the purpose of destroying the world."
O King, a portion of Kali was born from the womb of Gāndhārī—
impatient, fickle, wrathful, and difficult to appease;
by the power of destiny, his brothers were likewise born with such traits.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya.
Śakuni was his maternal uncle, and Karṇa was his dearest friend.
Eleven thousand and eight kings have arisen together on this earth for the sake of its destruction.
As the king is born, so shall his people become;
if the master is righteous, unrighteousness turns into righteousness.
"Servants take on the virtues and faults of their master; of this there is no doubt.
Having encountered a wicked king, O monarch, your sons have perished.
O mighty-armed one, Nārada knows this matter according to its true nature."
"O lord of the earth, your sons have perished through their own transgression.
Do not grieve for them, O Indra among kings, for there is no cause for grief.
Indeed, O Bhārata, those Pāṇḍavas have committed no offense, however slight."
"Your sons are evil-minded, by whom this earth has been destroyed.
This was undoubtedly announced long ago by Nārada, may you be blessed,
in the assembly of Yudhiṣṭhira during the Rājasūya sacrifice."

"O Kaunteya, once the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas have encountered one another, they shall no longer exist; therefore, perform that which is your duty. Having heard these words of Nārada, the Pāṇḍavas then fell into mourning.

11,008.034c All this eternal secret of the gods has been told to you. 11,008.035a O Lord, how might your grief be destroyed, given your compassion for living beings and your affection for the sons of Pāṇḍu, once you have understood the ordinance ordained by fate?

"O mighty-armed one, this very matter was heard by me previously when it was recounted to Dharmarāja at the Rājasūya, the supreme of sacrifices. When the secret had been disclosed by me, the son of Dharma exerted himself [to conceal it]."
11,008.037c Even when the Kauravas were without a physical form [to fight], destiny was indeed more powerful.
11,008.038a For fate, O King, cannot be transgressed in any way; 11,008.038c for by the decree of the Ordainer, neither the stationary nor the moving beings [can escape].
O Bhārata, you who are devoted to action and possessed of the highest wisdom— even you are bewildered when considering the departure and arrival of living beings;
yet here you are, tormented by grief and repeatedly losing your composure.
Knowing this, King Yudhiṣṭhira would even renounce his own life;
for that hero is eternally compassionate, even toward those born as animals. O Indra among kings, how then could he not show compassion toward you?
"By my command alone, and because the decree of Fate is irreversible,
and out of compassion for the Pāṇḍavas, maintain your life, O Bhārata. As you conduct yourself in this manner, your fame shall spread throughout the world."

O dear one, this is a very great dharma, and it would be as if asceticism had been practiced for a long time; O Great King, always, always extinguish with the water of wisdom this fire of grief for your son that has arisen like a blazing flame.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra reflected for a moment and then spoke:
"O best of the twice-born, I am overwhelmed by a great web of grief."
"Deluded again and again, I do not recognize myself;
yet, having heard these words of yours born of divine decree,
I shall sustain my life-breaths and strive not to grieve."
Having heard these words, O king of kings, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
vanished right there before Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Janamejaya said:
11,009.001a When the Blessed Vyāsa had departed, what did King Dhṛtarāṣṭra do, O brahmin-sage? You should explain that to me.
11,009.001c Likewise, what did the high-minded Kuru king, the son of Dharma, do?
And what did those three, Kṛpa and the others, do?
We have heard of the deeds of Aśvatthāman and the mutual curses they inflicted upon one another.
Vaiśampāyana said:

11,009.001d@001_0004 Tell me the subsequent account of what Saṃjaya spoke, 11,009.001d@001_0005 now that Duryodhana has been slain and the entire army has been destroyed. 11,009.001d@001_0006 Saṃjaya said:
Saṃjaya, his wisdom departed, presented himself before Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O King, having arrived from various lands, the lords of diverse realms have all gone to the world of the ancestors along with your sons.
O Bhārata, O lord of the earth, while your son was constantly entreating him,
he caused the entire earth to be slaughtered— sons, grandsons, and fathers alike— in his desire to bring an end to the enmity.
"Perform all the funeral rites for them in the proper sequence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those terrible words of Sañjaya, the lord of the earth...
Motionless like one whose life had departed, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Approaching that lord of the earth as he lay upon the ground,
Vidura, the knower of all dharma, spoke these words.
"Arise, O King! Why do you lie there? Do not grieve, O bull of the Bharatas.
This indeed is the ultimate destiny for all beings in this world; O Bhārata, beings begin in non-existence and have existence as their middle state."
Since all things indeed end in non-existence, what cause for lamentation is there?
A man does not follow the dead by grieving, nor does he die by grieving. Since this world is thus established by its very nature, why do you grieve?
One who does not fight may die, and one who fights may live;
O Great King, when the time has arrived, no one can transcend it. Time drags away all beings, indeed all various kinds of creatures.
O best of the Kurus, there is no one who is dear to Time, nor anyone who is hateful.
Just as the wind sweeps away the tips of blades of grass from every side,
so do all beings fall under the power of Time, O bull of the Bharatas.
For all those traveling together as one caravan toward the same destination,
when the time for departure comes first for one among them, what cause is there for lamentation?
And as for those whom you mourn in battle, O King—
For those high-souled ones are not to be grieved for; they have all gone to the third heaven.
Neither by sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, nor by austerities, nor by sacred knowledge do men attain heaven in the same way as the heroes who cast off their bodies in battle.
All were knowers of the Vedas, all were heroes, and all had fulfilled their vows;
yet all have perished facing the enemy—what cause for lamentation is there? Into the fires of the bodies of those heroes, they offered oblations of arrows.
Even while being struck by arrows, those supreme men endured them.
Thus, O King, I have described to you this most excellent path leading to heaven;
for a Kṣatriya in this world, nothing exists that is superior to battle.
Those high-souled Kṣatriyas were heroes who graced the assembly;
having attained the highest blessings, they are all indeed not to be grieved for. Having comforted yourself by means of your own self, do not grieve, O bull among men.
"Overcome by grief as you are today, you ought not to abandon your duty.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, O best of men, he reflected for a long time and became unconscious.
Having said, "Yoke Sañjaya," he addressed Vidura.
Upon hearing those words of Vidura, that bull among men,
having said, "Let the vehicle be readied," spoke these words again.
"Bring Gandhārī quickly, along with all the women of the Bharata lineage,
taking Kuntī, your daughter-in-law, and whatever other women are there.
Having spoken thus to Vidura, the most knowledgeable in dharma, that righteous-souled one—
His wisdom struck down by grief, he pursued the vehicle alone.
And Gāndhārī, afflicted with sorrow, urged on by her husband’s words,
rushed together with Kuntī and the other women toward where the king was.
Having approached the king, they were overwhelmed with intense grief;
having addressed one another, they then went forth and wailed aloud.
Vidura comforted them, though he himself was even more afflicted than they.
Having placed those with tearful throats upon the vehicles, he then departed from the city.
Thereupon, a great cry arose in all the Kuru dwellings;
the entire city, including the children, became emaciated with grief.
Those women who had never before been seen even by the hosts of gods were then seen by common folk when their lords had been slain;
they scattered their beautiful hair and cast off their ornaments.
Wearing but a single garment, the women fled like those who are helpless;
they emerged from their houses, which resembled white mountains,
like female deer with their herd-leaders slain fleeing from mountain caves.
Then, O King, those numerous throngs of women,
overwhelmed by grief like young fillies in a courtyard,
rushed forth crying out and raising their arms, wailing for their sons, brothers, and even their fathers.
They seemed to manifest the destruction of the world at the end of an eon;
lamenting and weeping, they ran hither and thither,
their wisdom struck down by grief, not knowing what ought to be done.
Those women who formerly felt shame even before their friends,
now stood before their mothers-in-law wearing but a single garment and devoid of modesty;
they who used to offer mutual consolation in even the most trivial sorrows.
Overwhelmed by grief, O King, they looked only at one another. Surrounded by those thousands of weeping women, the king,
dejected, went forth quickly from the city toward the field of battle.
Artisans, merchants, Vaiśyas, and those who subsist by all kinds of labor—
placing the king at their head, they went out from the city as those distressed women cried out during the destruction of the Kurus.
A great sound arose, causing even the worlds to tremble,
like that of living beings being consumed by fire when the end of the age has arrived; all creatures thought, "This dissolution has come."
With their minds deeply agitated at the destruction of the Kurus, those citizens,
who were intensely devoted to them, cried out loudly at that time, O great king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone from there for the distance of a *krośa*, they beheld those great car-warriors:
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat; the son of Droṇa; and Kṛtavarman.
Upon seeing the king, their lord whose wisdom is his eye, they [stood before him].
With throats choked with tears, sighing and weeping, they said this:
"O Great King, your son, having performed a most difficult deed,
has gone, O Lord of the Earth, to the world of Śakra accompanied by his followers."
"O bull of the Bharata race, only we three chariot-warriors have escaped from Duryodhana's forces; all the rest of your army has been utterly destroyed.
Having spoken thus to the king, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then—
He spoke these words to Gāndhārī, who was afflicted with grief for her sons:
"Fighting fearlessly and slaying many hosts of enemies,
your sons have met their end while performing heroic deeds."
Having attained those stainless worlds won by the sword,
they dwell like immortals, having assumed radiant bodies;
for all those heroes, facing their enemies, were slain while fighting.
For among heroes fighting in battle, there is none who has met his end with a weapon while turning his back, nor is there anyone who did so with palms joined in supplication; this,
they say, is the ancient and supreme goal of a Kṣatriya.
They met their end by the sword in battle; you ought not to grieve for them.
Furthermore, O Queen, those Pāṇḍava enemies have not achieved success against them.
Hear what has been accomplished by us, led by Aśvatthāman.
Having heard that your son had been slain unrighteously by Bhīmasena,
and that he had entered the camp while it was asleep and wrought a slaughter among the Pāṇḍavas,
[they learned] that all the Pañcālas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, had been killed.
The sons of Drupada and the sons of Draupadī have been struck down. Having thus slaughtered that host of your sons and enemies,
we three fled from the battle, for we were unable to remain there.
For those heroic Pāṇḍavas, great archers, will soon arrive,
overcome by indignation and desiring to avenge their enmity,
having heard that their sons— those bulls among men— were slain while they were heedless.

"O illustrious lady, desiring to quickly reach our destination, we heroes cannot bear to remain here after having brought disgrace upon the Pāṇḍavas. Grant us your permission, O Queen, and do not set your mind on grief."
"O King, grant us leave; maintain the highest fortitude.
Behold also the ultimate end and the singular duty of a Kṣatriya.
Having spoken thus to the king and having circumambulated him clockwise, [he departed].
O Bhārata, Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Droṇa—
those high-souled ones, looking toward King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the wise one,
quickly urged their horses along the Ganges.
But having departed, O King, all those great car-warriors,
having taken leave of one another in their agitation, then set out in three directions.
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then went to Hastināpura.
Hārdikya went to his own kingdom, and the son of Droṇa went to the hermitage of Vyāsa.
Thus those heroes departed, looking at one another,
afflicted by fear after having committed an offense against the high-souled sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having assembled around the king before the sun had risen,
O great king, those heroic subduers of enemies then departed as they pleased.
Then, having encountered the son of Droṇa, the great car-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu—
O King, having displayed their prowess immediately thereafter, they were victorious in battle.
Vaiśampāyana said: When all the armies had been slain, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma—
He heard that his aged father had departed from Hastināpura;
afflicted by grief for his son,
he then set out toward him who was overwhelmed by grief for his son, mourning together with his brothers, O Great King.
Pursued by the high-souled hero of the Daśārhas,
by Yuyudhāna, and likewise by Yuyutsu,
Draupadī followed him, afflicted with great sorrow and emaciated by grief.
Accompanied by the Pāñcāla women who had gathered there,
O best of the Bharatas, he beheld along the Gaṅgā crowds of women wailing like distressed female ospreys.
Surrounded by those thousands of weeping women with their arms upraised, who were distressed and speaking of what was dear and what was not dear, [the king thought]:
"Where now is the king’s knowledge of dharma? Where now is his compassion?"
When you slew fathers, brothers, teachers, sons, and even friends;
and having caused Drona and Bhishma, your grandfather, to be slain— O mighty-armed one, what was the state of your mind after killing Jayadratha as well?
"O Bhārata, what use have you for kingship, seeing neither your fathers nor your brothers, nor the invincible Abhimanyu, nor the sons of Draupadī? Having passed them by,
O mighty-armed one, they are crying out like female ospreys."
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, paid homage to his eldest father. Then,
having saluted their father according to dharma,
those Pāṇḍavas, the subduers of their enemies, each announced their names in full.

Afflicted by the slaughter of his son, the father— displeased and tormented by grief— embraced that Pāṇḍava who had brought about the end of his own offspring. Having embraced Dharmarāja and consoled him, O Bhārata, [he spoke].
That evil-minded one sought out Bhīma like a fire desiring to consume everything;
that fire of his anger, fanned by the wind of his grief,
appeared as if it wished to burn down the forest that was Bhīmasena.
O King, having perceived Bhīma’s wicked intention, Hari—
the one of unwearied deeds— first had that iron image brought back,
which had previously been fashioned by Duryodhana.
On the stage of fitness, for the sake of exertion, he mentally directed his attention toward Bhīma;
having seized Bhīma with both hands, he offered him the iron Bhīma.
But the highly intelligent Hari had already perceived his intention beforehand.
The highly wise Janārdana made his arrangements there. But the powerful king, thinking him to be Vṛkodara, seized that iron Bhīmasena with both hands and broke it.
Possessing the strength and vitality of ten thousand elephants, that king, having shattered the terrible iron [stake],
had his chest mangled and blood flowed from his mouth;
then he fell upon the earth, drenched in blood just as he was.
Then the learned Sūta Gāvalgaṇi embraced him, who was like a *pārijāta* tree with its topmost branches in full bloom;
he spoke to him, saying "Do not do this," as if pacifying and consoling him.
Casting off his anger and freed from resentment, that high-minded one, overcome once more by grief, cried out repeatedly, "Alas! Alas!
Bhīma! Perceiving that he was now devoid of wrath, though still tormented by the thought of Bhīmasena’s death, [he spoke].
Vāsudeva, the best among men, spoke these words:
"Do not grieve, Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this Bhīma was not slain by you.
For it was an iron image, O King, that was struck down by you."
"O bull of the Bharatas, knowing that you had fallen under the sway of anger,
I drew back the son of Kuntī, who had entered the very jaws of death.
For there is no one at all, O tiger among kings, who is your equal in strength."
O mighty-armed one, what man could endure the restraint of your arms? Just as no one, having encountered the God of Death, escapes alive,
so too no one could live after coming within the range of your arms.
"Therefore, O Kauravya, this iron image of Bhīma which was caused to be made by your son has been brought here by me for you alone;
for my mind has been led away from dharma by the intense heat of grief for my son."
"O Indra among kings, it is because of that [debt] toward you that you desire to slay Bhīmasena. But that is not fitting for you, O King, that you should kill Vṛkodara;
for your sons, O great king, could not survive in any way."
"Therefore, whatever we have done, considering it to be appropriate, please grant us your forgiveness for all of that; do not set your mind on grief.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then attendants approached him for the purpose of purification;
and once he had performed his ablutions, Madhusūdana spoke to him again:
"O King, you have studied the Vedas and various treatises."
You have heard the Purāṇas and the entire body of royal duties (*rājadharma*).
O highly wise one, knowing this, you did not then follow that advice,
even though you were capable of discerning strength and weakness.

"O Bhārata, why do you harbor such anger due to your own transgression? At that very time, I spoke to you, as did Bhīṣma and Droṇa, as well as Vidura and Saṃjaya; yet you, O King, did not act upon it."

Though he was being restrained, O Kaurava, he did not heed us, knowing the Pāṇḍavas to be superior in both strength and heroism. For that king who possesses steady wisdom perceives his own faults himself.
He who understands the distinction between place and time attains the highest good; but he who, when being instructed, does not grasp what is beneficial regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome,
falls into calamity and grieves, being established in misconduct.
"Therefore, O Bhārata, look upon yourself as being of a different character;
for you, O King, being one whose self is unsubdued, remain under the power of Duryodhana. Since you are distressed by your own transgression, why do you wish to kill Bhīma?"

Therefore, restrain your anger, reflecting upon your own misdeed. That base man who, out of rivalry, brought the Pāñcālī into the assembly hall has been slain by Bhīmasena, who sought to avenge their enmity.
"Behold your own transgression and that of your evil-minded son,
O scorcher of foes, in that you have abandoned the sinless Pāṇḍavas.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, O lord of men, he admitted that everything was true.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to the son of Devakī:
"O mighty-armed Mādhava, it is exactly as you say. However, O righteous-souled one, affection for my son has shaken my fortitude."
"By good fortune, O Kṛṣṇa, that tiger among men, powerful and of true prowess, protected by you, did not come within the reach of my arms. Now,
however, I am single-minded, my anger gone, and my fever subsided."
"O Keśava, I wish to touch the heroic middle Pāṇḍava. Now that the lords of kings have been slain and my sons have been killed,
peace and joy abide within me through the sons of Pāṇḍu."
Then, weeping, he touched with his own limbs the well-limbed Bhīma, Dhanañjaya, and the two sons of Mādrī, those heroes among men.
Having comforted them, he spoke auspicious words to them.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, permitted by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those bulls among the Kurus—
All the brothers, together with Keśava, approached Gāndhārī.
Then, having learned that Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira had slain his enemies,
the blameless Gāndhārī, afflicted by grief for her sons, desired to pronounce a curse.
Having perceived her evil intention toward the Pāṇḍavas,
the seer who was the son of Satyavatī had already become aware of it beforehand.
Having touched the pure water of fragrant merit in the Gaṅgā, he—
The supreme ṛṣi, possessing the speed of thought, arrived at that place;
seeing with his divine eye and with an undisturbed mind,
he perceived there the inner state of all living beings.
At the proper time, that man of great asceticism, who spoke with auspicious greetings, addressed his daughter-in-law; setting aside the time for the curse, he uttered words of peace:
"O Gāndhārī, you must not harbor anger toward the Pāṇḍavas; attain tranquility."
"Restrain this passion; hear these words of mine. For eighteen days you have been addressed by your son, who desires victory:
'O mother, pray for my welfare as I fight with the enemies.'"
"O Gāndhārī, though you were thus entreated from time to time by me, who desired victory, you replied: 'Where there is dharma, there is victory.
And I, O Gāndhārī, have not made your past words false."
O illustrious lady, do not set your mind on anger now that my words have passed;
I remember you as you were speaking, for you were so intent.
O auspicious daughter of Subala, I remember you even in your private moments.

Having reached the further shore in the tumultuous conflict of kings without doubt, the sons of Pāṇḍu have surely been victorious in battle; therefore, Dharma is surely superior. Having previously been of a forgiving nature, why do you not forgive now?
"O knower of dharma, abandon unrighteousness; for where there is dharma, there is victory.
Therefore, O wise Gāndhārī, having remembered the dharma and spoken these words with your voice, restrain your anger; do not be thus, O speaker of truth."
Gāndhārī said:
"O Blessed One, I do not harbor ill-will toward them, nor do I wish for their destruction;
yet my mind is as if overwhelmed by force through grief for my sons."
Just as the sons of Kuntī must be protected by Kuntī, so must they be protected by me;
just as they must be protected by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so must they be protected by me,
due to the transgressions of Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
This destruction of the Kurus was brought about by Karna and Duḥśāsana;
neither Bībhatsu, nor Vṛkodara the son of Pṛthā,
nor Nakula, nor Sahadeva, nor indeed Yudhiṣṭhira ever committed any offense.

For the Kauravas, fighting and cutting one another down, were slain together by others; in that matter, there is nothing disagreeable to me. However, as for the deed that Bhīma performed while Vāsudeva was looking on—
Having challenged Duryodhana to a mace-duel, the high-minded Bhīṣma—
knowing him to be superior in training as he moved in various ways on the battlefield—
struck him below the navel; that increased my wrath.
"How indeed could heroes, for the sake of their lives, ever abandon in battle the Dharma as it has been proclaimed by the high-souled ones who know the Dharma? Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of hers, Bhīmasena, then as if struck with fear,
replied to Gāndhārī with these conciliatory words:
"Whether it was unrighteousness or righteousness, that which was done by me there was out of terror."

"Desiring to save myself, you ought to forgive me for that. Indeed, that son of yours, possessed of great strength, could not have been overcome by anyone through righteous combat; therefore, I acted unfairly."

"Previously, Yudhiṣṭhira was defeated by him through unrighteous means, and we were always treated with deceit; therefore, he acted unfairly. This one warrior remains of the army, and he is valiant in combat with the mace."
"I did this so that, having killed me, he would not seize the kingdom;
and as for the princess of Pañcāla, clad in a single garment and in her courses—
your son has told you everything that was known to you."

"Without having subdued Suyodhana, it is not possible for us to enjoy the earth with its oceans in its entirety; therefore, this was done by me. Furthermore, your son committed an act toward us that was most unpleasant."
"Because he displayed his left thigh in the midst of the assembly before Draupadī,
that evil-doer, your son, O Mother, deserved to be slain by us right then and there;
yet we remained bound by our agreement at the command of Dharmarāja."
"O Queen, that great enmity was fanned by your son;
we were constantly tormented in the forest, and therefore this was done by me. Having slain Duryodhana in battle, I have reached the end of this enmity."
"Yudhiṣṭhira has obtained the kingdom, and we have been freed from our grief.
Gāndhārī said:
"My son, this is not his slaughter, as you praise it to me."
And you have indeed performed all that which you have spoken to me regarding Nakula when his horses were slain by Vṛṣasena, O Bhārata— that you drank the blood born from Duḥśāsana’s body in battle.
"O Vṛkodara, why did you perform such a cruel deed— terrible, censured by the virtuous, practiced only by ignoble men, and improper? Bhīmasena replied:
One must not drink the blood of another, much less one's own.
Just as one’s self, so too is a brother; there is no difference whatsoever between them.
Mother, do not grieve; my blood has not passed beyond my teeth and lips.
"Vaivasvata knows that; my hands are stained with blood. Do not take that to heart, O mother, for it was not drunk by me, O sinless one, when I saw Nakula’s horses slain by Vṛṣasena in battle."

I have instilled fear in my brothers who were filled with joy; however, because I made a sign saying "I am drinking blood in anger," let there be no grief for me, for the blood did not even reach my teeth or lips.
"You cannot drink my blood at the forefront of battle;
you are a fool roaring in vain, like a cloud devoid of water. While your small-minded son was speaking thus, [the earth trembled].
"My heart was pierced and my blood drunk by the Rākṣasī who was my wife;
yet I did not make the vow, 'I shall drink the enemy's blood.
[This occurred] during the seizing of Draupadī’s hair at the gambling match."
"O Queen, that which I spoke out of anger still dwells within my heart:
'May I fall from the dharma of the Kṣatriyas for eternal years'—
it was with that vow unfulfilled that I performed those deeds."
"O Gāndhārī, you ought not to suspect me of fault;
for previously, you did not restrain your sons while we remained free from harm.
But now, why indeed should you suspect me of fault?"
Gāndhārī said:
"O unconquered one, why did you not leave even a single one of this old man's hundred sons alive,
when some among them had committed only a slight offense?"

"O dear one, why has this single staff not been spared for us two, who are aged, deprived of our kingdom, and blind? For while you, O dear one, remain as the survivor among our sons, you are the only support for these two blind men."
"11,014.022c This would not be a source of sorrow for me, if you were to practice righteousness.
11,015.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Gāndhārī questioned Yudhiṣṭhira.

Afflicted by the slaughter of her sons and grandsons, she cried out in anger, "Where is that king? Then the lord of kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, approached her and spoke these sweet words to her.
"O Queen, I am Yudhiṣṭhira, the cruel slayer of your son;
I am worthy of a curse, having become the cause of the earth's destruction—curse me!
For I have no need for life, nor for kingdom, nor for wealth."
"Having slain such friends, this fool who betrays his kin—
toward him who was speaking thus, terrified and standing close by, Gāndhārī, sighing heavily and incessantly, did not say anything at all."
As King Yudhiṣṭhira, with his body bowed, was about to fall at her feet, that queen— knower of dharma and seer of dharma—
beheld the tips of his toes through the opening of her garment.
Then that king, whose nails had become deformed,
having seen him, Arjuna went behind Vāsudeva.
O Bhārata, as they were thus maneuvering here and there, [the enemy]—
Gāndhārī, her anger having subsided, comforted them like a mother. Having been granted permission by her, those broad-chested heroes went together to their mother Pṛthā, the mother of warriors.
Having seen her sons after a long time, the queen, overwhelmed by anxiety for her children,
covered her face with her garment and shed tears.
Then Pṛthā, together with her sons, released her weeping.
She saw them, grievously mangled in many ways by the floods of weapons. Touching each of those sons again and again, she,
afflicted with grief, lamented for them and for Draupadī whose children had been slain.
Then he saw the princess of Pañcāla weeping, fallen upon the ground.
Draupadī said:
"Noble lady, where have all those grandsons of yours gone, together with the son of Subhadrā?"
"They do not come to you today, for you, an ascetic woman, have not been seen for a long time. What indeed is the use of a kingdom to me, deprived as I am of my sons?
Vaiśampāyana said:
The large-eyed Pṛthā comforted Yājñasenī,
who was weeping and emaciated by grief, having raised her up;
and Pṛthā, accompanied by her, followed along with her sons.
Even more afflicted than the distressed Gāndhārī, she herself approached her.
Then Gāndhārī spoke to that illustrious daughter-in-law:
"O daughter, do not be thus; overcome with grief as you are, look upon me as well, for I am suffering."

"I believe this destruction of the world, impelled by the turn of time, has arrived as an inevitable occurrence; it is hair-raising by its very nature. These great words of Vidura have now come to pass."
Since Kṛṣṇa’s persuasion was unsuccessful, that which the high-minded one said must now be accepted;
for when that unavoidable matter has passed, especially so, do not grieve, for those who met their death in battle are not to be mourned.
"Just as you are, so am I; who indeed will comfort me?
For it is through my own transgression that this foremost lineage has been destroyed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, Gāndhārī, standing there, beheld with her divine eye the entire slaughter of the Kurus;
she was a devoted wife, highly blessed, and one who practiced vows identical to those of her husband.
Endowed with fierce ascetic power and always speaking the truth, she—
by virtue of a boon granted by the great seer Kṛṣṇa of meritorious deeds—
possessed divine knowledge and strength as she lamented in various ways.
That wise woman beheld from afar, as if it were close at hand,
the wondrous and hair-raising battlefield of those heroic men—
a field strewn with bones and hair, and flooded with torrents of blood.
It was strewn on all sides with many thousands of bodies; it was covered with the corpses of elephants, horses, chariots, and warriors, fouled with blood,
along with headless trunks and heaps of headless heads.

It was strewn with the lifeless bodies of elephants, horses, and heroic men; it was frequented by jackals, vultures, crows, herons, and ravens; it was a place of delight for man-eating *rakṣasas* and filled with ospreys.
Resounding with both inauspicious and auspicious cries, and frequented by vultures;
then, permitted by Vyāsa, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and all those sons of Pāṇḍu, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, [proceeded].
Placing Vāsudeva at their head and approaching the king whose kinsmen had been slain,
the Kuru women proceeded toward the field of battle.
Having reached Kurukṣetra, those women found themselves with their lords fallen.
There they beheld their sons, brothers, fathers, and husbands slain,
being devoured by flesh-eaters— jackals, crows, and vultures—
as well as by various spirits, *piśācas*, *rakṣasas*, and night-stalking demons.
Then, seeing that slaughter-ground resembling the playground of Rudra, the women,
crying out, fell from their costly vehicles;
the wives of Bharata, afflicted by grief, beheld what they had never seen before.

Some fell upon the bodies [of others] without stumbling, while others fell to the ground; for those who were exhausted and leaderless, there was no consciousness at all. That great and piteous sight occurred among the women of the Pañcālas and the Kurus.
Having seen that most terrible battlefield, which resounded on all sides with the cries of those whose hearts were stricken by grief, the daughter of Subala, who knew the Dharma,
then addressed the lotus-eyed one, the Supreme Person.
Having witnessed the slaughter of the Kurus, he spoke these words out of grief:
"Behold them, O lotus-eyed Mādhava— my daughters-in-law whose lords have been slain,
with disheveled hair, wailing like female ospreys."
Having come together and remembering those bulls of the Bharata race,
they ran separately toward their sons, brothers, fathers, and husbands.
O mighty-armed one, the field was crowded with women who had given birth to heroes, yet whose sons had been slain.
In some places it was crowded with the wives of heroes whose husbands had been slain;
it was adorned by tigers among men— Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Abhimanyu— and by Droṇa, Drupada, and Śalya, who were like blazing fires.
It was adorned with golden armor, gold neck-ornaments (*niṣka*), and jewels belonging to the great-souled ones;
it was further embellished with armlets, bracelets, and garlands,
as well as with spears and iron clubs hurled by the arms of heroes.
With stainless, sharp swords, and with arrows and bows,
throngs of delighted flesh-eaters stood together in some places,
while in others they were sporting about, and still others lay down.
"O hero, O Lord, behold this very battlefield in such a state;
yet, O lotus-eyed one of great splendor, this deed has been accomplished by you.
And as I look upon it, O Janārdana, I am consumed by grief."

O Madhusūdana, I did not think of the slaughter of the Pāñcālas and the Kurus— the destruction of these two groups— as if they were merely the five elements. Suparṇas and vultures are now dragging them away, drenched in blood.
Having seized them by the armor, those fierce beings devour them by the thousands.
Who would dare to contemplate the destruction of Jayadratha, Karṇa, as well as Droṇa and Bhīṣma, and Abhimanyu?
O Madhusūdana, seeing those who were nearly invincible now slain—
reduced to food for vultures, herons, crows, hawks, dogs, and jackals—
I have fallen under the sway of indignation, even though they remained under the command of Duryodhana.
Behold these tigers among men, who were once like extinguished fires; all accustomed to soft and spotless beds,
they now lie upon the bare earth, having met their end.
Constantly greeted at the proper times by bards singing their praises,
they now hear various auspicious yet inauspicious and terrible voices.
Those illustrious heroes who formerly lay upon royal beds now lie [upon the earth].
Those whose limbs were once anointed with sandalwood and aloe now lie in the dust;
over their ornaments, these inauspicious and terrible vultures, jackals, and crows shriek again and again as they snatch them away.
Bows, yellow-feathered arrows, stainless swords, and bright maces— those who took pride in battle carry these as if they were alive with joy;
many of them, possessing handsome forms and complexions, lie there, mangled by flesh-eating beasts.
With eyes resembling those of a bull and wearing green garlands, they lie there;
others, however, with arms like iron clubs,
lie facing their maces as heroes embrace their beloved wives.
Others, wearing bright armor and carrying stainless weapons,
do not allow the flesh-eaters to attack them, O Janārdana, thinking, "They are still alive.
As for other great-souled ones being dragged away by the flesh-eaters, [the others protect them].
11,016.039c Colorful garlands made of gold are scattered everywhere.
11,016.040a These fearsome jackals are snatching by the thousands the necklaces from the throats of the illustrious fallen warriors.
Those whom the bards— trained in the highest praises and ritual services— used to delight with their hymns during all the final watches of the night,
those very men these most excellent women now lament, afflicted by grief.

"O tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, it is piteous; O Keśava, the faces of these excellent women, severely afflicted by pain and grief, appear truly beautiful even as they are parched, like groves of red lotuses."

Having ceased their weeping, these Kuru women, overwhelmed with grief and lost in thought, approach him here and there in their distress. These [limbs] are the color of the sun and resemble refined gold.
Behold, O Keśava, the throngs of Duryodhana’s noble women— dark-complexioned ones of excellent hue, fair-skinned ones, and those clad in single garments— their faces copper-red with rage and weeping.
Sprinkled repeatedly with tears and saliva, and drenched by sprays of water,
it is now being bathed by the tears from the eyes of Duryodhana’s noble women.
Having heard their lamentations, which reveal that their purpose remains unfulfilled—
Because they are distracted by their mutual cries, the women do not perceive [the danger].
Having heaved long sighs, cried out, and lamented,
these heroes, quivering with grief, abandon their lives.
Seeing many bodies, they cried out and lamented;
others, with tender hands, struck their own heads,
as heads, hands, and all limbs lay scattered in heaps.
The earth shines, strewn with bodies intermingled with one another; seeing those headless trunks that take delight in the terrible [battle],
as well as the bodiless heads, the women, unaccustomed to such sights, faint away.
Joining their heads to their bodies, they gazed about, deprived of their senses;
unable to see the other parts there, they were distressed, thinking, "This is not that.
Others saw arms, thighs, and feet, severed by arrows and scattered apart.
Overwhelmed by misery, they repeatedly fainted as they tried to identify one another;
yet, seeing others with their heads severed or devoured by beasts and birds,
some of these women of Bharata could not recognize their husbands.
And others, O Madhusūdana,
seeing their brothers, fathers, sons, and husbands slain by the enemy,
struck [the foe] with their hands; [the ground was covered] with arms still clutching swords and with heads adorned with earrings.
O best of the Bharatas, the earth became as if impassable, a mire of flesh and blood, filled with living beings deprived of life; those blameless ones,
who had never before known suffering, now plunged into misery.

O Janārdana, behold the numerous throngs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s daughters-in-law— women with beautiful hair— who, like herds of young mares, have covered the earth along with their brothers, fathers, and sons.
"O Keśava, what indeed appears more painful to me than this, that all these women display such various forms? Surely some evil deed was committed by me in previous births."
"O Keśava, I see my sons, grandsons, and brothers slain"—
thus, distressed and lamenting, she beheld her son lying dead after addressing Janārdana.
Gāndhārī, afflicted with grief for her sons and emaciated by sorrow,
lay upon the hero’s bed.
11,017.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, seeing Duryodhana, Gāndhārī, emaciated by grief,
suddenly fell to the ground like a plantain tree cut down in the forest.
Having regained consciousness, she cried out again and again;
then, seeing Duryodhana lying there drenched in blood,
Gāndhārī embraced him and lamented piteously.
"Alas, alas, my son! she lamented, her senses overwhelmed by the pain of grief.
Tormented by sorrow, she drenched with the water of her tears his broad chest, which was marked by well-formed clavicles and adorned with necklaces and golden coins.
Standing nearby Hṛṣīkeśa, he spoke these words:
"O Lord, when this battle for the destruction of kinsmen had begun,
this best of kings, with palms joined in reverence, said this to me, O Vārṣṇeya."
"In this joy of our kinsmen, let my mother proclaim victory for me.
When this was said, I—who knew all the arrival of my own calamity—spoke thus: "Since Kṛṣṇa is on [our] side, therefore there will be victory."
"O tiger among men, I said: 'Where there is dharma, there is victory.
O son, so that you do not lose your composure while fighting, you shall surely attain, O lord, the worlds won by weapons, like an immortal."
"I did not speak thus previously, O Lord; indeed, I do not grieve for him.
But I grieve for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who is wretched now that his kinsmen have been slain—for he was intolerant, the best among warriors, skilled in weapons, and fierce in battle."
"Behold my son, O Mādhava, lying upon the bed of heroes—
this scorcher of foes who used to go at the head of all consecrated kings,
yet now lies here in the dust; behold the reversal brought by Time."
Surely the heroic Duryodhana has attained a state difficult for us to reach;
for he lies facing the enemy upon a bed frequented by heroes— upon that very bed which excellent women used to delight him as they sat around him in the past.
Inauspicious jackals delight him as he lies upon the hero’s bed—
those very ones whom, in former times, kings delighted while sitting around him.
Now that he has been struck down and lies upon the surface of the earth, vultures sit around him.
He whom women formerly fanned with the finest fans,
today birds fan him with their wings. This mighty-armed, powerful one of true valor now lies here.
Like an elephant in battle felled by a lion, Duryodhana has been struck down by Bhīmasena; behold him, O Kṛṣṇa, lying there drenched in blood,
slain by Bhīmasena with his mace raised, O Bhārata.
O Keśava, he who formerly led eleven akṣauhiṇīs in battle, that mighty-armed one has now met his end through misfortune. Here lies Duryodhana, the great archer and great chariot-warrior.
Like a tiger brought down by a lion, he was struck down by Bhīmasena.
For this dull-witted man, having disregarded Vidura and his own father, this fool, through his contempt for the elders, has fallen under the power of death.
"He for whom the earth remained without a rival for thirteen years—
he, my son, the lord of the earth, lies slain upon the ground.
O Kṛṣṇa, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, I beheld the earth [desolate]."
"O Vārṣṇeya, that abundance of elephants, cattle, and horses was not long-lasting.
O mighty-armed Mādhava, today I see that very same [city] under the command of another, bereft of elephants, cattle, and horses; why indeed do I still live?"
"Behold this even more grievous sight than the slaughter of my son himself:
that these women sit around the heroes slain in battle— this lady of beautiful hips with disheveled hair, who once rested in the embrace of Duryodhana’s arms."
"O Kṛṣṇa, behold Lakṣmaṇa’s mother, who resembles a sacrificial altar of gold. Surely, in the past, while the mighty-armed one was still living,
this wise woman used to delight in embracing his beautiful arms."
Why does this heart of mine not shatter into a hundred pieces,
as I behold my son slain in battle along with his own son?
The blameless woman is now smelling her son, who is drenched in blood.
The lady with beautiful thighs stroked Duryodhana with her hand;
why indeed does this high-minded woman grieve for her husband and her son?
For she appears thus situated even as she gazes upon her son.
O Mādhava, striking her own head with her five fingers, the large-eyed lady fell upon the chest of the Kuru king, the hero;
shining like a white lotus, she possessed the radiance of the interior of a lotus.
Having wiped the face of her son and that of her ascetic husband, she said:
"If there are indeed sacred scriptures and likewise the Vedas,
then this king has surely attained those worlds won by the strength of his own arms."
Gāndhārī said:
"Behold, O Mādhava, my hundred sons, who had conquered all fatigue,
mostly slain in battle by Bhīmasena with his mace."
"This is even more painful for me today, that these young daughters-in-law of mine— whose hair is disheveled, who have lost their sons in battle—
are running about, they who used to walk upon the floors of palaces with feet adorned with ornaments."
11,018.003c Since they have fallen, touching this earth drenched with blood;
11,018.004a And since they drive away the vultures, jackals, and crows,
11,018.004c Afflicted by grief and reeling, they wander about like those intoxicated.
This other woman of faultless limbs, whose waist is as slender as a palm,
having seen that terrible slaughter,
falls down in extreme distress upon seeing this daughter of a king, the mother of Lakṣmaṇa.
"O mighty-armed one, my mind finds no peace regarding the princess.
Seeing their brothers, other wives, and sons slain upon the earth, these women, with their fair arms, run about while clutching one another's arms."

O unconquered one, hear the lamentation of the middle-aged and aged women whose kinsmen have been slain during this terrible slaughter— [the cries] from the seats of chariots and the bodies of the fallen elephants and horses.
"O one of great strength, behold them standing there, overcome by exhaustion and delusion;
and see another who, O Kṛṣṇa, stands holding the head of her own kinsman— his body stripped of its beautiful earrings and high nose."
"O sinless one, I believe the evil committed in my previous births was not small, since we,
along with these blameless women and myself of little wit,
have been brought here by Dharmarāja, O Janārdana."
For there is no destruction, O Vārṣṇeya, of good and evil deeds. Behold these women of fresh youth, with beautiful breasts and bellies,
born in noble families, modest, with dark-limbed eyes and hair.
"Behold them, O Mādhava, fallen like female cranes crying out in distress, their voices faltering like those of swans, utterly bewildered by pain and grief.
O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, the faces of these women shine like full-blown lotuses."
