The sun, with its unpleasant rays, scorches the faultless faces of my sons— who were once jealous, possessed the pride of rutting elephants, and looked down upon the inner apartments of Vāsudeva— now that they are mere commoners.
Hundred-mooned shields, banners resembling the sun, golden armor,
and golden neck-ornaments—
these helmets of my sons lie upon the surface of the earth.
"Behold, O Govinda, these blazing fires like well-offered oblations.
Here lies Duḥśāsana, struck down by the heroic slayer of enemies,
Bhīmasena, with all his limbs drenched in blood."
"Behold my son, O Mādhava, with this hero-slaying mace!
Remembering the sufferings of the gambling match and urged by Draupadī,
he spoke thus to the princess of Pañcāla when she had been defeated at dice in the assembly hall."
O Janārdana, desiring to do what is pleasing to his brother and to Karṇa, [he said]:
"Together with Sahadeva, Nakula, and Arjuna, you are the wife of slaves, O Pāñcālī; enter our house at once."
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, I spoke to King Duryodhana:
"O son, avoid Śakuni, who is already ensnared by the noose of death. Understand this evil-minded maternal uncle, who is so fond of strife."
"Quickly abandon him, my son, and make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
You do not realize, O evil-minded one, that Bhīmasena is intolerant;
you are piercing him with sharp word-arrows as if striking an elephant with flaming torches."
11,018.026a Holding fast to those sharp arrows of speech, this impetuous and cruel man released his venom upon them, like a serpent upon bulls.
11,018.027a Here lies Duḥśāsana, with his two massive arms outstretched.
Slain by Bhīmasena like a great bull by a lion,
his face still possessed the sleep born from the touch of the pleasure of union with his beloved;
yet the exceedingly intolerant Bhīmasena acted with extreme ferocity.
11,018.028c When he was enraged in battle, he drank the blood of Duḥśāsana.
11,019.001 Gāndhārī said:
11,019.001a O Mādhava, here is my son Vikarṇa, who was esteemed for his wisdom.
Slain by Bhīma and cut into a hundred pieces,
he lies upon the ground; Vikarṇa, O Madhusūdana, lies amidst the elephants like the sun in autumn surrounded by dark clouds.
This great hand of his, scarred by the grasping of his bow and protected by a leather guard,
is being torn with difficulty by vultures eager to devour it. His ascetic wife [is trying to ward off] these vultures who seek his flesh.
O Mādhava, though he constantly restrains her, the young girl does not obey him.
O bull among men, that youth Vikarṇa— handsome, brave,
accustomed to comfort, and worthy of happiness— now lies upon the dust, O Mādhava.
Even now, Fortune does not abandon this best of the Bharatas, whose vital organs were pierced in battle by barbed, reed-tipped, and iron-headed arrows.
This was done by that hero in combat, who was intent on fulfilling his vow.
Durmukha, the slayer of enemy hosts, lies facing the foe, slain in battle;
O Kṛṣṇa, his face, half-devoured by beasts of prey,
shines all the more brightly, my dear, like the moon on the seventh day.
O Kṛṣṇa, how is it that my son, a hero whose face shone thus in battle even when half-devoured by beasts of prey,
now lies slain by his enemies, swallowing the dust?
O gentle Madhusūdana, how was that Durmukha— who could not possibly stand at the front of battle— slain by his enemies, he who conquered the world of the gods? Citrasena lies slain upon the ground.
Behold this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the very model of all archers.
Young women, emaciated by grief, accompanied by throngs of flesh-eating beasts, sit around him weeping, though he is adorned with variegated garlands and ornaments.

The sound of women weeping and the roaring of wild beasts— this wondrous sight, O Kṛṣṇa, appears most strange to me. [He who was] ever a youth, a god among men, and attended by the most excellent women.
"O Mādhava, there lies Vivimśati, destroyed in the dust;
his armor mangled by arrows, that hero slain in the slaughter,
twenty vultures sit surrounding him, encircling Vivimśati."
Having entered the army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle,
the hero has once again entered a bed worthy of a virtuous man;
he who possesses a smile, a beautiful nose, and lovely eyebrows, resembling the lord of the stars.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the exceedingly radiant face of Vivimśati,
whom thousands of celestial maidens used to attend upon like Vasu attended by the wives of Vāsava, or like a Gandharva sporting with divine nymphs.
Who could withstand Duḥsaha— the slayer of heroic armies, a hero who graces the assembly, the destroyer of enemies?
This body of Duḥsaha appears thus, covered with arrows.
Like a mountain covered with blossoming *karṇikāra* trees growing from its own body,
he shone with his golden garland and radiant armor;
like a white mountain, though lifeless, he remained unbearable as if filled with fire.
Gāndhārī said:
O Mādhava, O Daśārha, they say that he who was described by his father and by you as possessing one-and-a-half times the qualities of strength and heroism, is like a haughty, fierce lion.
"He who alone shattered my son's army, which was difficult to break—
having become the death of others, he himself has fallen under the power of death.
O Kṛṣṇa, I perceive this regarding that son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna), who possesses immeasurable splendor."
"Even though Abhimanyu has been slain, his radiance does not fade at all.
This daughter of Virāṭa, the daughter-in-law of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— this distressed, young, and blameless woman laments for her heroic husband who is now to be pitied."
11,020.005a For this daughter of Virāṭa, O Kṛṣṇa, having approached her husband who was nearby, 11,020.005c stroked him with her hand;
11,020.006a the illustrious lady, having smelled the face of that son of Subhadrā.
Her neck is as rounded as a conch shell, and her face has the form of a full-blown lotus;
this beautiful woman embraces him with a longing form,
yet she is bashful as before, fainting from the intoxication of the honeyed wine.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having removed his armor— which was smeared with blood and adorned with gold— she gazes upon his body.
O Kṛṣṇa, looking toward him, that young woman addresses you."
"O lotus-eyed one, this man, whose eyes were like yours, has been struck down.
O sinless one, he was equal to you in strength, heroism, and splendor;
now, surpassed even by you in beauty, he lies fallen upon the earth."
"O you who are exceedingly delicate and accustomed to reclining on the skins of Rāṅkava deer,
does your body not suffer today when lying upon the bare ground? Your arms are as massive as the trunks of elephants, and their skin has been hardened by the constant drawing of the bowstring."
Having cast down your two massive arms, adorned with golden armlets, upon Śeṣa,
you surely lay there as if having slept soundly after much exertion and fatigue;
yet you do not speak to me, though I lament thus in my distress.
"I do not recall any offense of yours; why do you not speak to me?
Surely, in the past, upon seeing me from afar, you would address me, as well as my noble sister Subhadrā and these [brothers] who resemble the gods."
"Where will you go, leaving behind your ancestors and me, who am afflicted with grief?
Raising his blood-stained hair with her hand and placing his face upon her lap as if he were still alive, she asks him:"
The vultures sit around him— the nephew of Vāsudeva, the son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the grandson of Maghavan himself.
"How did these great car-warriors slay you while you stood in the midst of battle? Fie on those cruel doers— Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Jayadratha—
and on both Droṇa and the son of Droṇa, by whom you were brought to such calamity!"
What was the state of mind then of all those bulls among chariot-warriors,
who, surrounding you alone— a mere child— struck you down for my sorrow,
while the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas looked on?
O hero, though you possessed protectors, you have met your end like one who is helpless. Seeing you slain like one without a protector amidst the cries of many,
how can that heroic Pāṇḍava, a tiger among men, continue to live?
Neither the vast acquisition of a kingdom nor the defeat of enemies will bring such joy to the sons of Pṛthā as you, O lotus-eyed one,
except for the worlds won by your weapons through righteousness and self-restraint.
"I shall return quickly; wait for me there.
It is difficult for anyone to die before their time has come, since I, though wretched, still live after seeing you slain in battle."

O tiger among men, whom will you now address with gentle words and a smile, having gone to the world of the ancestors, as you did to me? Surely you will captivate the hearts of the apsarases in heaven.
Having attained the worlds of the merit-makers with supreme beauty and speech preceded by smiles, and having united there with the Apsarases,
O son of Subhadrā, while sporting there in due time, you shall remember my good deeds.
"11,020.026a This much was the dwelling ordained for you here with me; 11,020.026c six months [have passed], and in the seventh month, O hero, you have met your end.
11,020.026d Having gone to the third heaven, O you of auspicious conduct, you should remember Subhadrā."

When she had spoken these words, the women of the Matsya royal household dragged away the sorrowful Uttarā, whose hopes were now in vain; having dragged away the afflicted Uttarā, they themselves became even more afflicted.
Seeing Virāṭa slain, they cry out and lament;
these vultures, jackals, and crows are pecking at Virāṭa, who lies there mangled by the arrows of Droṇa’s weapons and drenched in blood.
Though Virāṭa was being pecked by the birds, those dark-eyed women,
helpless and distressed, were unable to turn him away;
for these women were already scorched by the heat of the sun and exhausted by their exertion.
The bodies of those who were once fair have lost their luster due to exhaustion;
behold these slain youths— Uttara, Abhimanyu, Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sudarśana.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava, behold Lakṣmaṇa of pleasing appearance, struck by the son of Kṛṣṇa (Kārṣṇi), lying in the very midst of the front of the battlefield. Gāndhārī said:

11,021.001a Here lies Vaikartana, that great archer and mighty chariot-warrior; 11,021.001c like a blazing fire extinguished in battle by the splendor of Pārtha. 11,021.002a Behold Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, who, having slain many great car-warriors, now lies here.
His limbs drenched in a flood of blood, he lies fallen upon the earth;
that intolerant and long-resentful hero, a great archer and mighty car-warrior,
now rests slain in battle by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Those great car-warriors, my sons, who out of fear of the Pāṇḍavas used to fight placing him at their head like elephants following a leader of the herd,
have now encountered Savyasācin in battle like a tiger encountering a lion.
O tiger among men,
the wives of that hero, who had been slain in battle, have gathered together and sit weeping around him, their hair disheveled— like an elephant struck down by a maddened elephant.
Because Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was constantly anxious,
he did not obtain sleep for thirteen years while reflecting upon it;
he is unassailable by enemies in battle, like Maghavan himself.
Resplendent like the fire at the end of an eon and as steadfast as the Himalayas,
that hero, having become the refuge of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, O Mādhava,
now lies slain upon the earth like a tree uprooted by the wind.
Behold Karṇa’s wife, the mother of Vṛṣasena,
lamenting piteously and weeping as she lies fallen upon the ground;
surely the preceptor’s curse has followed you.
Since this earth was once turned by you into a supreme wheel,
therefore your head has been struck off by Dhananjaya with an arrow in the midst of the enemy in battle.
"Alas! Woe! This one has fallen unconscious," they said, beholding the gold-adorned breastplate of the long-armed Karṇa, whose spirit was undaunted.
Suṣeṇa’s mother, weeping and deeply afflicted, [said]:
"For that great-souled one has been reduced to a mere remnant by the flesh-eaters who were devouring his body."
Like the moon on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, she was no longer pleasing to behold;
turning back, she fell upon the earth.
Rising up once more in distress, she,
tormented by the slaughter of her son, repeatedly sniffs the face of Karṇa and wails piteously.
Gāndhārī said:
The vultures and jackals devour the hero of Āvantya, who was struck down by Bhīmasena; though he had many kinsmen, they treat him as if he were friendless.
Behold him, O Madhusūdana, who, having wrought a slaughter of his enemies,
now lies upon a hero’s bed, drenched in blood;
around him are jackals, vultures, and various kinds of flesh-eating beasts.
"With this and that [cord] they drag him away; behold the revolution of Time!
The women sit weeping all around the Avanti prince, a hero who moved through the cries of battle, now lying upon the bed of heroes."
"Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the high-minded Bāhlika of the Prātipīya clan, that great archer, slain by my broad-headed arrow and lying like a sleeping tiger;
even though he has been struck down, the complexion of his face remains exceedingly radiant."
Like the full moon rising on the day of the full moon,
Vṛddhakṣatra was struck down in battle by the son of Pākaśāsana, who, though tormented by grief for his son, remained steadfast in keeping his vow.

Behold this Jayadratha, the lord of Sindhu and Sauvīra, full of pride and high-minded, slain by one who has conquered eleven armies and desired to fulfill his vow, even while he was being protected by that great-souled one.
O Janārdana, jackals and vultures are devouring Jayadratha,
O Acyuta, even as he is being protected by his devoted wives;
barking, they drag him away from the vicinity toward a deep thicket.
These [women] wait upon that mighty-armed one, guarding him;
Duḥśalā guards the human [son],
guarding that mighty-armed one.
O Janārdana, when Jayadratha fled with the women of Sindhu, Sauvīra, Gāndhāra, Kamboja, and Yavana, taking Kṛṣṇā along with him and accompanied by the Kekayas,
at that very moment Jayadratha became worthy of death at the hands of the Pāṇḍavas.
When Jayadratha was released by those who honored Duḥśalā,
why, O Kṛṣṇa, do they not honor her today?
This very daughter of mine, a young girl, is lamenting in great distress.
He brings about his own destruction and reviles the Pāṇḍavas. O Kṛṣṇa, what indeed could be more painful for me than this: that my young daughters-in-law, their husbands slain, have become widows?

"Alas! Look at Duḥśalā, who seems as if free from grief and fear, running here and there without reaching her husband's head. He who restrained all the Pāṇḍavas, though they were longing for their son—"

Having destroyed vast armies, he himself has fallen under the power of death. Surrounding that hero, who was like an elephant in rut and exceedingly difficult to conquer, these women with faces like the moon are weeping.
Gāndhārī said:
"O dear one, here lies Śalya, the maternal uncle of Nakula himself, slain in battle by the righteous Dharmarāja, who knows the dharma."
"O bull among men, this very one who was always vying with you in every respect—
this great car-warrior, the King of Madra— lies here slain.
Even if they were to attribute some fault whatsoever to Jayadratha,"
How could those wishing to speak of his transgression against the son of Madra do so,
O dear one, when by seizing the chariot of the son of Adhiratha in battle,
he thus brought about the destruction of [Karna’s] prowess for the sake of the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu?
"Alas! Behold the face of Śalya, as beautiful as the full moon, with eyes like lotus petals—once free of blemish, now bitten by vultures.
And this [hand] of him who had the luster of gold, shining like refined gold..."
His tongue, protruding from his mouth, is being devoured by black birds. The women of the Madra royal house sit weeping around Śalya, that ornament of assemblies, who was slain by Yudhiṣṭhira.
Clad in very fine garments, these Kṣatriya women, having approached the bull among men, the king of Madra, cried out as they stood surrounding Śalya, that bull among Kṣatriyas, who had fallen.
Like a bull submerged in the mud,
behold this hero, the best of chariot-warriors, the giver of refuge, Shalya,
lying upon the bed of heroes, his body mangled by arrows.
This is King Bhagadatta, the powerful Śailālaya,
the foremost wielder of the elephant-goad; he lies prostrate upon the earth, struck down,
while this golden garland still shines resplendent upon his head.
As he was being devoured by beasts of prey, his hair seemed as if it were adorning him;
it is said that with this creature, Pārtha had a most terrible battle,
hair-raising and exceedingly fierce, like that of Śakra against Bala.
Having fought Pārtha Dhanañjaya and brought him to a state of peril, this mighty-armed one was struck down by the son of Kuntī—
he to whom no one in the world is equal in heroism and prowess.
11,023.014c This very Bhīṣma, the doer of terrible deeds in battle, lies here slain.
11,023.015a Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, the son of Śantanu lying there, radiant as the sun,
11,023.015c like the sun brought down from the sky by Time at the end of a Yuga.
"O Keśava, this heroic sun among men, having scorched his enemies in battle with the heat of his weapons, now goes to his setting, just as the sun sets; this hero,
who was equal to Devāpi in righteousness, lies upon a bed of arrows."
Behold him lying upon a hero’s bed, frequented by the brave— having spread his excellent couch with barbed, calf-toothed, and iron-headed arrows,
the Blessed One lies there as Skanda entered the forest of reeds.
Filled with no cotton, yet provided with three arrows as its pillow—
the finest of pillows— this was offered by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow; and he,
of great fame, remaining chaste and observing his father’s command, protected it.
11,023.020c This son of Śantanu lies here, O Mādhava, peerless in battle;
11,023.021a righteous-souled and knower of dharma, O dear one, through his traditional discernment, 11,023.021c though being mortal, he has maintained his life-breaths like an immortal.
There is no one skilled in battle, no scholar, and no man of prowess,
where Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, now lies slain by his enemies—
having been questioned in person by this very hero, the Pāṇḍavas.
Death in battle was declared by that knower of dharma, the speaker of truth;
he by whom the perished Kuru lineage was raised up once again—
that one of great intelligence has met with defeat along with the Kurus.

"O Mādhava, now that Devavrata— the bull among men, equal to a god— has gone to heaven, whom indeed will the Kurus consult regarding matters of dharma? [Whom shall they ask] the teacher who was the instructor of Arjuna as well as of Sātyaki?"
Behold Drona, the best of the preceptors of the Kurus, fallen there—
he who knew the fourfold weapons just as the Lord of the Thirty-three [Indra] does,
or as the highly powerful Bhargava did, O Madhava.

Through whose grace the Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu performed deeds difficult to accomplish, he now lies slain; his weapons did not protect him. Placing whom at their head, the Kurus used to challenge the Pāṇḍavas.
This Drona, the best among weapon-bearers, has been severed limb from limb by weapons;
he whose movement while consuming the enemy host was like that of fire now lies slain upon the earth, like a fire whose flames have been extinguished.
O Mādhava, the grip on the bow and the hand-guard of Drona remain unbroken,
appearing as if he were still alive;
for from him, O Keśava, came the four Vedas and all weapons.

These two auspicious ones, worthy of praise and already lauded by bards, have not strayed from their heroic nature since the very beginning of Prajāpati; yet now, jackals drag at those feet which were once honored by hundreds of disciples.
"O Madhusūdana, Kṛpī, her consciousness overwhelmed by grief, sits wretchedly beside Droṇa, who has been slain by the son of Drupada.
Behold her weeping, afflicted, with disheveled hair and face cast downward."
O Keśava, that ascetic woman with matted hair, who attends upon Droṇa— the best of weapon-wielders— now sits by her slain husband in battle,
his armor pierced by the arrows of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Distressed and miserable, the illustrious and delicate Kṛpī strives to perform the funeral rites for her husband slain in battle;
having brought the sacred fires according to the rules, she kindles the pyre on all sides.
Having placed Droṇa upon it, the chanters of the Sāmans sing the three Sāman hymns;
and these matted-haired celibates scatter over the funeral pyre bows,
spears, and chariot-seats, O Mādhava.
They will burn that one of great splendor with various other weapons;
having placed Drona upon the funeral pyre, they both praise him and weep,
while others chant the three *Sāman* hymns situated within.
Having offered the *droṇa* vessel into the fire as if placing fire within fire,
the twice-born disciples of Droṇa proceeded toward the Gaṅgā;
keeping the funeral pyre to their left, they then placed Kṛpī at their head.
Gāndhārī said:
Behold the son of Somadatta, struck down by Yuyudhāna;
he lies near the descendant of Madhu, being pecked by many birds.
"O Janārdana, Somadatta, tormented by grief for his son,
appears as if he were reproaching the great archer Yuyudhāna.
And there is Bhūriśravas’s mother, overwhelmed with sorrow."
The blameless woman comforted her husband Somadatta:
"By good fortune, O great king, you do not behold this terrible destruction of the Bharatas,
this horrific slaughter of the Kurus, which resembles the end of an eon."

"By good fortune, you do not see today that hero, the son who bore the sacrificial post as his banner, the giver of many thousands, the performer of numerous sacrifices, slain [in battle]. By good fortune, you do not hear the many terrible lamentations of your daughters-in-law in their cries of distress."
O Great King, you do not hear [the cries] like those of female cranes upon the ocean: your daughters-in-law,
clad in single garments with their black hair disheveled,
run about, their children slain and their lords killed.
"Alas, by good fortune you do not see him being devoured by beasts of prey—
this tiger among men, whose arm was severed and who was struck down by Arjuna;
nor do you see Śala slain in battle, nor Bhūriśravas."
"By good fortune, you do not see here today all those widowed daughters-in-law;
by good fortune, you do not see that golden umbrella of the high-souled son of Somadatta, which was scattered upon the seat of the chariot."
But those dark-eyed wives of Bhūriśravas, having surrounded their husband who had been slain by Sātyaki, were mourning him; these women,
emaciated by grief for their lord, lamented profusely.
"Alas, O Keśava, they fall face-down upon the ground in a miserable state! How could Bibhatsu have committed this most loathsome deed—
that he severed the arm of that heroic sacrificer while he was distracted?"
"Then Sātyaki committed an even more sinful deed,
since he struck one who was seated in *prāya* (fasting unto death) and possessed of a disciplined soul. You, though righteous, lie there slain by two through unrighteousness."
"What indeed will he say among the virtuous, in social gatherings, and in assemblies—
that this Satyaki himself has committed this unmeritorious and disgraceful deed?"—
thus these women of Yūpadhvaja cry out, O Mādhava.
This is the wife of Yūpadhvaja, whose waist is measured by the span of a hand;
resting her arm upon her husband’s lap, she lamented piteously:
"This is that [arm] which used to pull up my girdle and press against my full breasts."
This hand, which touches the navel, thighs, and hips, and loosens the knot of the lower garment;
this hand is the slayer of enemies and the bestower of fearlessness upon friends;
it is the giver of thousands of cows and the bringer of the end to the Kṣatriyas.
While he was fighting in battle against another, distracted, and in the very presence of Vāsudeva, he was struck down by Pārtha of unwearied deeds;
what indeed will you say in assemblies and in conversations, O Janārdana?
"Either Arjuna’s great deed or the Diademed One himself [performed it]. Having thus reproached her, that beautiful woman remains silent;
her co-wives grieve for her as if she were their own daughter-in-law.
Śakuni, the powerful King of Gāndhāra, whose valor was true,
has been slain by Sahadeva— his own maternal nephew—
after having formerly been fanned with two gold-handled fans.
He who used to assume forms by the hundreds and thousands is now lying here being fanned with wings by birds;
the illusions of that master of magic have been consumed by the fiery energy of the Pāṇḍava.

He who, through deceit, won from Yudhiṣṭhira his vast kingdom in the assembly hall by means of trickery— O Kṛṣṇa, that Śakuni has now been defeated and even his life is lost; birds are gathering around Śakuni from all sides.
This gambler was trained for the destruction of my sons;
by him this great enmity with the Pāṇḍavas has been instigated,
leading to the slaughter of my sons, as well as of himself and his followers.
"O Lord, just as worlds won by weapons belong to my sons,
so too do worlds won by weapons belong to this evil-minded man.
And why is it that he does not go there with my sons and his brothers?"
O Madhusūdana, that crooked woman would oppose those of upright intellect,
since she sits there wretchedly, afflicted by grief for her sister Kṛṣṇā;
she constantly desires the destruction of my sons and is filled with rage toward me.
Gāndhārī said:
"O Mādhava, behold the invincible Kāmboja, who was accustomed to a Kāmboja carpet; see him lying in the dust, slain, with shoulders like those of a bull."
11,025.002 Her arms, once smeared with sandalwood paste, are now stained with blood;
seeing them, her husband’s wife laments piteously, overwhelmed by extreme sorrow.
11,025.003 These are those two arms, resembling iron clubs, with their beautiful palms and fingers.

"O Lord of Men, deprived of you, what state shall I now go to— like one whose kinsmen are far away, like one who is helpless, and possessing a voice that was once so exceedingly sweet? Formerly, delight did not leave me even when I had fallen into the interval between those two."
Like various garlands withering in the heat,
the beauty does not indeed desert the bodies of these women, even though they are exhausted.
O Madhusūdana, [behold] the Kalinga hero lying there surrounded by them.
"Behold, O Janārdana, Jayatsena, the lord of the Magadhas, whose great arms are bound by a pair of blazing armlets;
behold the women of Magadha weeping as they surround him."
O Janārdana, the sound of these women— whose eyes are wide,
whose voices are melodious, and who are now weeping, emaciated by grief, with all their ornaments cast aside— captivates both the mind and the ear, as if it were bewildering my very soul.
The women of Magadha lie upon the ground, though accustomed to well-spread beds;
surrounding their husband, Prince Bṛhadbala, the sovereign of the Kosalas, these women weep individually.
Overcome by distress and fainting again and again, they extract the arrows from his body that were struck there by the strength of Kṛṣṇa’s arms;
for all these faultless women, exhaustion has set in from the heat of the sun.
O Mādhava, their faces shine like withered lotuses;
slain by Droṇa, heroes adorned with beautiful armlets lie prostrate.
All the young sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, wearing golden garlands, lie there as well.
The chariot was its fire-chamber, the bow its flame, and the arrows, spears, and maces its fuel;
having reached Droṇa, they were consumed like moths in a fire.
In that same way, the slain heroes lay there, adorned with beautiful armlets.
All five Kekaya brothers,
clad in armor of refined gold and possessing copper-colored banners, chariots, and garlands, faced Droṇa;
blazing with splendor, they illuminated the earth like flaming fires.
"Behold Drupada, O Mādhava, struck down by Droṇa in battle like a great elephant in the forest slain by a mighty lion— behold the vast,
pale white [umbrella] of the Pāñcāla king, O lotus-eyed one."
The royal parasol shines like the sun in autumn.
But these daughters-in-law and wives, afflicted with grief, having cremated the aged Drupada, go around the Pāñcāla king keeping him to their left.
The women, their hearts stolen away, carry off the heroic Dhṛṣṭaketu, that great archer and bull among the Cedis, who was slain by Droṇa; for he,
O Madhusūdana, was struck down by Droṇa’s weapon in the midst of the fray.
"Thus has the son of my son followed his father here;
that great archer lies slain like a tree swept away by a river.
This is the heroic lord of Cedi, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the great chariot-warrior."

Slain in battle after killing his enemies by the thousands, he lies prostrate; O Hṛṣīkeśa, his wives have approached the King of Cedi as he is being pecked at by birds, having been killed along with his army and kinsmen.
Placing upon their laps the hero born of the daughter of the Daśārhas— who lies there, possessed of true prowess— these excellent women of the Cedi king weep;
O Hṛṣīkeśa, [they mourn] his son, who had a handsome face and beautiful earrings.
Behold him, O Madhusūdana, cut into many pieces by Droṇa’s arrows in battle;
surely even now he does not abandon his heroic father as he fights with the enemies on the field of combat from behind.
"Even so, O mighty-armed one, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, has followed his father Duryodhana as my son has followed his own father.
Behold Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti fallen, O Mādhava!"
Like two *śāla* trees in bloom at the end of winter, stripped bare by the wind,
those two— clad in golden armlets and armor, wielding arrows, swords, and bows, with eyes like those of a bull and wearing spotless garlands— lay there.
"O Kṛṣṇa, all the Pāṇḍavas, together with you, are invincible—
those who have escaped from Droṇa and Bhīṣma, from Karṇa Vaikartana, from Kṛpa,
from Duryodhana, from the son of Droṇa, and from the great car-warrior Saindhava."
From Somadatta, Vikarṇa, the heroic Kṛtavarman, and others—
those bulls among men who could slay even the gods with the force of their weapons— these very men have been slain in battle; behold the reversal brought by Time.
"O Mādhava, there is certainly no burden too heavy for destiny,
since these heroes— bulls among Kṣatriyas— have been slain by other Kṣatriyas;
my sons were brave, learned, and high-minded."
At that very moment, O Kṛṣṇa, my powerful sons were as good as slain,
when you returned to Upaplavya with your desires unfulfilled,
along with the son of Śantanu and the wise Vidura.
"Right then, O Janārdana, I was told: 'Do not feel affection for your own children.
Therefore, dear one, it cannot be that those two have not been seen;
my sons must have been reduced to ashes long ago."
11,025.034 Vaiśampāyana said: Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, Gāndhārī, emaciated by grief and her consciousness overwhelmed by sorrow, cast off her fortitude and fell to the ground.
Then, her limbs overwhelmed by anger and her senses distressed by grief for her son, Gāndhārī went to Śauri with a sense of grievance. Gāndhārī said:

"O Kṛṣṇa, Janārdana, why did you, while remaining capable, possessed of many followers, and stationed within a vast army, overlook the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras as they injured one another and were perishing?"
O Madhusūdana, since the destruction of the Kurus was desired and overlooked by you, who were capable of acting in both cases and possessed of the sacred word,
O mighty-armed one, therefore receive the fruit of that.
"O self-controlled one, bearer of the discus and mace, by whatever merit I have acquired through service to my husband, with that I shall curse you,
for the kinsmen— the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas— are slaying one another."
"O Govinda, because you have been indifferent toward them, you shall therefore slay your kinsmen.
O Madhusūdana, when the thirty-sixth year has arrived, you too,
having had your kinsmen slain, your ministers slain, and your sons slain, will wander in the forest."
Unknown like one who is helpless, unremarked among the worlds,
you shall meet your end through a contemptible means;
likewise for you, your sons will be slain and your kinsmen and relatives killed.
"11,025.042c These women will fall into distress, just like these women of the Bharatas.
11,025.043 Vaiśampāyana said:
11,025.043a Having heard those terrible words, the high-minded Vāsudeva—

11,025.043c He spoke to Queen Gāndhārī, as if smiling slightly: 11,025.044a "O auspicious lady, there is no one other than myself who can destroy the Vṛṣṇi host; I know this very well, yet you act in this manner, O Kṣatriya woman."
"By fate alone the Vṛṣṇis shall perish; there is no doubt in this. They are incapable of being slain by other men, nor even by gods or Dānavas;
therefore, the Yādavas will meet their destruction at each other's hands."
When the descendant of Daśārha had spoken thus, the Pāṇḍavas became terrified in heart;
they were deeply agitated and lost all hope for their lives.
Vāsudeva said:
"Arise, arise, O Gāndhārī; do not set your mind on grief.
For it was indeed through your own fault that the Kurus met their destruction—you who [favored] a son who was evil-minded, envious, and excessively arrogant."
Placing Duryodhana at your head, you consider your own evil deed to be virtuous; cruel, harsh in its enmity, and transgressing the commands of the elders—
how can you wish to cast the blame for your own actions upon me?
He who grieves over what is past— whether it be dead or lost—
obtains sorrow through sorrow and encounters two misfortunes. This Brahmin woman, seeking ascetic merit, bears a child in her womb.
The cow seeks the one who carries her; the mare, the one who runs; the Śūdra woman, the slave; and the Vaiśya woman, the cattle-herder;
but a princess such as you seeks only one worthy of slaughter.
11,026.006 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those unpleasant words spoken again by Vāsudeva,
Gāndhārī, her eyes agitated with grief, became silent.
But the royal seer Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having restrained the darkness born of ignorance,
that righteous soul questioned Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma:
"O Pāṇḍava, you are one who knows the total number of the living troops."
"If you know the number of those who have been slain, tell it to me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ten times ten thousand, another ten thousand, and twenty thousand more."
Eleven thousand, two hundred and six crores,
as well as fourteen thousand, ten hundred, sixty-five others— these were the heroes slain in this battle of kings, O Indra among kings, whose names could not be discerned.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Yudhiṣṭhira, what destination have those best of men reached?
To which worlds indeed have these foremost of men gone?"
"Tell me, O mighty-armed one, those who were slain in battle while fighting and those who did not turn their backs, for you are considered by me to be omniscient.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

Those of true prowess who, with joyful hearts, offered their bodies as oblations in the supreme battle, have gone to worlds equal to those of the King of the Gods. But those, O Bhārata, who with a joyless mind thought only of the necessity of dying—
Those who were killed in battle while fighting, having encountered the Gandharvas, [attained their goal]. But those who, standing on the field of battle, begged for mercy with their backs turned,
and met their end by the sword, went to the Guhyakas.

Slain according to the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*), they have gone to the supreme goal. But those great-souled ones who, being oppressed by enemies, deprived of weapons, and lacking means of retreat, were restrained by their sense of shame and faced their foes in battle— [they too have attained the highest state].
Though being cut by sharp weapons, those heroes of great luster, who were devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriyas, went to the abode of Brahmā when slain; O King,
so it was with those who were killed there within the field of battle.
"O King, by whatever means they have reached the Northern Kurus.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"By what power of knowledge, my son, do you see thus like one who has attained perfection?"
"O mighty-armed one, tell me that if it is indeed something I may hear.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Formerly, while wandering in the forest at your command, [I heard it]."
"In the course of my pilgrimage to sacred fords, this favor was obtained:
the celestial sage Lomaśa was seen, and from him I attained the power of recollection; indeed, in the past, through the yoga of knowledge, I also acquired divine vision."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Bhārata, as for those among these people who were here without protectors and those who had protectors—
will their bodies be cremated according to the prescribed rites?"
"For those who have no performers of their rites, nor those who have not maintained the sacred fires—
whom else should we serve, O dear one, given the vastness of our task? They whom the *suparṇas* and vultures drag hither and thither,"
"Yudhiṣṭhira, by their actions alone shall their worlds be determined.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus addressed, the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī—"
He gave instructions to Sudharmāṇa, Dhaumya, and the charioteer Sañjaya;
to the highly intelligent Vidura and the Kuru Yuyutsu;
and to all his servants and charioteers, headed by Indrasena.

"O sirs, perform for these [deceased] all the funeral rites in every respect, so that no body may perish like one who is helpless. By the command of the King of Dharma, the Kṣattṛ and the Sūta Sañjaya [acted accordingly].
Sudharmā, together with Dhaumya and Indrasena and the others,
[prepared] wood of sandal and aguru, as well as kālīyaka,
ghee, oil, perfumes, and linen garments.
Having gathered together highly precious materials and heaps of wood,
as well as crushed chariots and various weapons there,
they diligently constructed pyres for the principal lords of men.
They undisturbedly cremated them according to the rites prescribed by rule:
King Duryodhana, his more than hundred brothers,
and the kings Śalya, Śala, and Bhūriśravas.
O Bhārata, [he slew] King Jayadratha and Abhimanyu,
the son of Duḥśāsana and Lakṣmaṇa, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu,
Bṛhanta, Somadatta, and more than a hundred Sṛñjayas.
[He addressed] King Kṣemadhanvan, as well as Virāṭa and Drupada, Śikhaṇḍin the Pāñcālya, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
and the valiant Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas.
Kauśalya and the sons of Draupadī, Śakuni the son of Subala, Acala and Vṛṣaka, King Bhagadatta,
and Karṇa Vaikartana together with his intolerant son.
The great archers of the Kekayas and the mighty chariot-warriors of the Trigartas;
Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas and brother of Baka;
King Alambuṣa and King Jalasandha.
O King, having constructed funeral pyres for hundreds and thousands of other monarchs as well— those great archers— all of whom were cremated according to the prescribed rites,
they burned them with blazing fires fed by streams of clarified butter.
The funeral rites for the ancestors were performed for some of those great-souled ones;
they sang with *sāman* chants while others lamented for them. Amidst the sound of the *sāmans* and *ṛcs*, and the wailing cries of the women, [the scene unfolded].
A dejection came over all beings during the night. Those fires, smokeless, blazing, and radiant,
appeared like planets in the sky veiled by thin clouds.
And those who were there without protectors, having come from various lands—
he summoned them all and, having made them into heaps by the thousands,
he composedly piled them up with abundant wood soaked in oil.
At the command of the King of Dharma, Vidura caused them to be cremated. Having performed the funeral rites for them, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus,
placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at his head, proceeded toward the Gaṅgā.
11,027.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having reached the auspicious Gaṅgā, which is frequented by holy beings, possessing deep pools, embankments, vast marshlands, and great forests—
Having removed their ornaments, upper garments, and turbans,
and having cast off their variegated coats of mail, they entered the Gaṅgā.
Then, [they offered oblations] for their fathers, grandsons, brothers, and kinsmen.
All the Kuru women, weeping and deeply afflicted by grief, offered water oblations for their sons, grandfathers, and husbands; likewise,
those who knew the dharma performed the water rites for their friends as well.
While the water was being drawn by the wives of the heroes for their husbands,
the Gaṅgā became easy to ford and flowed forth even more abundantly. That [city],
resembling the great ocean, was now devoid of joy and lacking in festivities.
The bank of the Gaṅgā shone, crowded with the wives of heroes.
Then, O great king, Kuntī, suddenly emaciated by grief,
spoke these words to her sons while weeping in a low voice.
He who was that hero, the great archer, the leader of the leaders of chariot-divisions,
marked with the characteristics of a warrior, has been slain by Arjuna in battle. O Pāṇḍavas, he whom you consider to be the son of a Sūta, the son of Rādhā— [he too is gone].
He who shone in the midst of the army like the lordly sun,
who formerly fought against all of you along with your followers,
and who gleamed while drawing forth the entire force of Duryodhana— [he has been slain].
He who is that hero, the great archer of immense strength and prowess,
for whom there is no equal in valor anywhere upon this earth;
that hero who has always chosen glory on this world even at the cost of his own life.
"Perform the water-libation for that brother of unwearied deeds, who was true to his word, a hero, and never fled from battles;
for he was your eldest brother, born to me from the Sun."
Wearing earrings and armor, he was a hero with a splendor equal to the sun;
he was a constant giver to Brahmins, a worshiper, and a protector of virtuous conduct;
grateful and truthful, he was a great chariot-warrior among great chariot-warriors.
Proud yet humble in spirit, handsome and pleasing to behold, devoted to his lawful wife, illustrious, and always firm in his commands,
King Duryodhana is dedicated to the welfare of his entire kingdom.
"He was always my favorite, and indeed the protector of my sons.
Upon hearing these unpleasant words of their mother, all the Pāṇḍavas grieved even more for Karṇa and became exceedingly distressed.
Then that tiger among men, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, spoke to his mother like a hissing serpent; the hero said:
"That [battle] which had arrows for its waves, banners for its whirlpools, and mighty arms for its great sea-monsters..."
The great lake of mighty chariots was stirred by the sound of his palms;
having encountered the fall of his arrows, no one could stand except for Dhanañjaya.
How did that son of yours, who was formerly like the offspring of a god, come to be?

"How could you have covered with a garment him whose fierce heat of arm we all experience on every side? How could you have hidden like fire with a cloth that one of terrible arm-strength, whom the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra serve?"

O best among the powerful, no chariot-warrior other than Karṇa, the son of Kuntī, could withstand the strength of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow as it was displayed by us, nor the strength of all those mighty lords of the earth.

"He was our first-born brother, the best among all wielders of weapons. How did you give birth to him of such wondrous prowess at the very beginning? Alas! We have been undone by your concealment of the truth."
For we, along with our kinsmen, were already tormented by the death of Karṇa;
and now by the destruction of Abhimanyu, the slaughter of the sons of Draupadī,
the annihilation of the Pāñcālas, and the downfall of the Kurus.
Therefore, this hundredfold suffering has now touched me most intensely;
for grieving over Karṇa alone, I burn as if placed within a fire.
With Karṇa and Arjuna as my allies, I could have even conquered Vāsava himself.
"Indeed, nothing would have remained unattainable, even that which dwells in heaven;
nor would this terrible slaughter, which brings an end to the Kauravas, have occurred.
Having lamented thus at great length, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [fell silent].
O King, making a low sound, the lord slowly offered water for him.
Then, all the men and women standing there on every side during that water-offering ceremony suddenly broke into loud cries.

Then the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, lord of the Kurus, out of affection for his brother, had the women of Karṇa’s household, along with their belongings, brought there. That righteous-souled one then performed the funeral rites for him together with them.
"Alas! We have been undone by your concealment of the mantra. Out of ignorance, I have slain my eldest brother through this evil deed.
He performed for Karṇa every ritual according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees."
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the wise Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, having untiringly offered water according to the prescribed rites,
[lamented]: "By me, a sinner, this most excellent brother and kinsman has been struck down."
"Therefore, that secret which women keep in their minds shall no longer exist.
Having said this, he emerged from the waters of the Gaṅgā with his senses agitated;
O Bhārata, he emerged from the Gaṅgā together with his wife.
Accompanied by all his brothers, he sat down upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The wise man who hears this, endowed with faith and devotion,
to him the divine Nārāyaṇa grants his heart’s desire.
Whatever evil has been committed through thought, speech, or body—
by honoring one who knows the Purāṇas, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, one shall obtain happiness in this world.
And having liberated all worlds, one is honored in the realm of Indra.
